experiments.title: Stem-cell organoids
experiments.why: Organoids grown from human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are small 3-D models of human brain or heart tissue. Researchers use them to study diseases such as Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis in cells from patients. On the ISS, neural organoids cultured for 30 days had higher levels of maturation genes and lower levels of proliferation genes than ground controls. Cardiac progenitor spheres grew larger and proliferated more than on-orbit 1 g controls. Microgravity gives researchers a different growth condition for studying tissue maturation, disease-linked changes and possible risks to the nervous systems of astronauts.
customers: Pharmaceutical and biotech teams that use iPSC-derived organoids in drug discovery for neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's)
Academic stem-cell and neuroscience labs, and the disease foundations that fund them
Regenerative-medicine developers working on iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and other cell products
Space agencies and human-spaceflight programs that study risks to the central nervous system on long missions
Organoid and iPSC tool companies that need flight validation of their culture media, cassettes and assays

heritage.mission: Neural organoids on SpaceX CRS-19 (New York Stem Cell Foundation Research Institute, Scripps Research, National Stem Cell Foundation, Space Tango)
heritage.platform: ISS (Space Tango CubeLab, a small incubator that holds 37 C; the payload was stowed in the ESA Columbus Laboratory)
heritage.what_flew: iPSC-derived cortical organoids (donors with primary progressive MS and controls) and dopaminergic organoids (donors with Parkinson's disease and controls). Half of the samples had matched iPSC-derived microglia added. Each organoid sat in its own sealed cryovial with 1 mL of DMEM/F-12 medium buffered with 15 mM HEPES. The cultures were shipped to Kennedy Space Center at 4 C, then sealed and loaded into the 37 C CubeLab. They flew live and had no medium exchange for 30 days. They came back live, and the CubeLab was opened six days after undocking.
heritage.finding: After return, the organoids attached to dishes and grew networks of neurites. Flown cortical and dopaminergic organoids had lower levels of proliferation genes and higher levels of maturation genes than ground controls. This suggests faster maturation. The authors found minimal stress, inflammation or apoptosis, and no signs of hypoxia. Some secreted proteins, including IL1R1, were higher in flight only when microglia were present. The authors say the protein data lacked the power to show consistent differences. They measured about 12 mGy of radiation and concluded that microgravity, not radiation, was the main cause of the differences.

heritage.mission: BOARDS (Brain Organoid Advanced Research Developed in Space), NASA designation UCSD-ORG01, SpaceX CRS-18 (UC San Diego, Muotri lab, with Space Tango)
heritage.what_flew: More than 100 iPSC-derived human brain organoids for about one month in orbit. UC San Diego said four weeks; the ISS National Lab says about 30 days.
heritage.finding: The ISS National Lab reports that brain organoids flown to the station showed molecular changes linked to aging and neurodegeneration sooner than similar models on Earth. It quotes Muotri: "senescence happening in accelerated time". The ISS National Lab also reports a separate finding in Rett syndrome organoids flown to the ISS (the source does not name the mission). Normally dormant genetic elements became active and caused inflammation in astrocytes. This led to tests of lamivudine, an HIV drug, and to a clinical trial in Rett syndrome. These results come from ISS National Lab reports, not from a peer-reviewed flight paper we could find.

heritage.mission: MVP-CELL-03 (Emory University with Techshot), SpaceX CRS-20
heritage.platform: ISS (Techshot Multi-specimen Variable-gravity Platform, MVP, with an on-board 1 g centrifuge control)
heritage.what_flew: 3-D cardiac progenitor spheres made from human iPSCs, cryopreserved at -80 C in cryosyringes. On board, the cryosyringes were thawed in a 37 C thermoblock into CO2-independent medium and loaded into the MVP modules. This was not an automated thaw. The spheres were cultured at 37 C with medium exchange every other day, side by side in microgravity and at 1 g on the centrifuge. Some samples were fixed in RNAProtect after 3 days. Live cultures returned in warm storage after 22 days.
heritage.finding: Compared with the on-orbit 1 g cultures, spheres in microgravity were 3 times larger, had 20 times more nuclei and expressed more proliferation markers. Cardiomyocytes made in microgravity handled calcium better. After only 3 days, genes for proliferation, survival, cardiac differentiation and contraction were already higher. Returned spheres began beating again 2 to 3 days after they went into an incubator.

protocol.sample: iPSC-derived 3-D organoids made in the customer's lab. The reference case is cortical or dopaminergic neural organoids, with or without matched microglia, as on the 2019 ISS flight. Cardiac progenitor spheres are a second option. One organoid goes in each well, with matched patient and control lines spread across the cassette.
protocol.container: LELP-1 large-bay 24-well sealed culture cassette with about 1 mL of medium per well (the heritage flight used 1 mL per sealed cryovial). It connects to the bay fluidics, with reservoirs for medium, 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixative, PBS storage buffer, RNA stabilizer and waste. The bay provides BSL-2 triple containment.
protocol.launch_state: Live organoids in sealed wells with HEPES-buffered medium, loaded late, with the bay held at 37 C and powered through ascent. On the 2019 ISS flight the organoids were shipped at 4 C and flew live in a 37 C incubator. Option for cardiac spheres: launch cryopreserved at -80 C in the passive cassette and thaw automatically in orbit. On the 2020 heritage flight, the thaw was done by hand on board, so an automated thaw has no flight heritage.
protocol.light_gas: No light is needed except short LED exposures for imaging. There is no CO2 supply. Wells use HEPES-buffered medium (heritage: DMEM/F-12 with 15 mM HEPES) and a sealed air headspace, with no gas exchange during flight. On the 2019 flight, organoids in sealed 1 mL cryovials showed no signs of hypoxia after 30 days.

steps.action: The customer lab finishes the organoids (aggregation, regional differentiation, and microglia added where used). The batch is split evenly between the flight cassette and the ground-control cassette.
Organoids are shipped at 4 C to the integration site. The 2019 heritage team shipped to Kennedy Space Center at 4 C.

One organoid is loaded into each well with 1 mL of HEPES-buffered medium. The cassette is sealed and installed in the bay at a 37 C setpoint, and the bay stays powered from here on. Spare organoids from the batch are fixed on the ground as the launch baseline.
RUPAK launch with the bay held at 37 C. Logging of acceleration, temperature and radiation dose starts.
In-orbit checkout: seal and pressure check, then a brightfield image of every well as the in-orbit baseline.
Daily brightfield imaging of all live wells for organoid size and shape, timed outside robotic-arm moves. Fluorescence images are taken if the customer uses reporter lines.
Early time point: in 4 wells, the medium is pumped to waste and replaced with RNA stabilizer. The 2020 cardiac flight fixed samples in RNAProtect at day 3.

Optional half-medium exchange (0.5 mL) in the live wells from the medium reservoir. Skip it to match the no-exchange heritage protocol. The arm carries the bay to the central 40x microscope for high-resolution images of 2 to 4 wells.
Last full imaging round of all live wells.

End of culture. In 8 wells the medium is replaced with 4% PFA for histology. In 6 wells it is replaced with RNA stabilizer. 6 wells stay live in their own medium for return, and that medium carries the secreted proteins.
After about 4 hours of fixation, the PFA in the 8 histology wells is pumped to waste and replaced with PBS storage buffer to avoid over-fixation during the trip home.
The bay setpoint is ramped from 37 C to 4 C and held. Imaging and pumping stop during the ramp so power stays under the peak limit.
Deorbit and splashdown, with the bay held at 4 C on battery. The cassette goes to the customer's courier about 20 minutes after splashdown and reaches the lab at 4 C within 1 to 2 days.

sample_return.note: The organoids are fixed or RNA-stabilized in orbit on day 13, before deorbit, so re-entry and the 1 g trip home do not change the end-point. Fixed organoids are moved from PFA to PBS after about 4 hours to avoid over-fixation. Live-return wells are cooled to 4 C, the temperature the heritage team used to ship live organoids before launch. The 72-hour window from preservation to the lab is our planning value: about 1 day in orbit, about 20 minutes to handover, then 1 to 2 days by courier. In the 2019 heritage flight, the CubeLab was opened six days after undocking.

experiments.ground_control: An identical flight-spare large-bay module and 24-well cassette, filled from the same organoid batch on the same day and kept at 37 C in the customer's or the integrator's lab. It runs the same fluidics timeline: RNA stabilization on day 3, an optional exchange on day 7, PFA fixation and RNA stabilization on day 13, the swap from PFA to PBS, and the cool-down to 4 C. It runs a few hours behind the flight so it can replay the flight bay's temperature log, and it goes through the same 4 C hold and courier trip. Launch-baseline organoids fixed on day -1 show the starting state. The standard bay has no in-orbit 1 g centrifuge, so the only microgravity control is on the ground. Launch vibration, radiation and 1 g are not matched; the dosimeter and accelerometer logs are used to account for them.

module.basis: OUR ESTIMATE, not a source claim. We chose a large bay for two reasons. A 24-well cassette gives enough wells for patient and control lines plus several end-points: day-3 RNA-stabilized, day-13 fixed, day-13 RNA-stabilized and live return. The module also carries its own microscope and reagent reservoirs. The 5.3 kg is the sum of the listed items, under the 6.0 kg large-bay limit. Peak power comes during an imaging pass while the thermoelectric block holds 37 C: about 10 W for the microscope LED, camera and stage, 4 W for the pumps, 2 W for the controller and up to about 12 W for the thermoelectric block. That makes about 28 W, under the 30 W large-bay limit. The ramp from 37 C to 4 C (thermoelectric block up to 25 W plus 2 W for the controller, about 27 W) runs with no imaging or pumping.

needs: The bay must stay powered at 37 C from cassette sealing on day -1, through integration, the launch pad and ascent, because the organoids launch live. This late-load, powered-ascent service goes beyond a passive cryo launch.
The bay must hold 4 C on battery through deorbit, splashdown and handover, and a 4 C insulated courier shipper must be ready on the recovery ship.
Robotic-arm moves and attitude manoeuvres must be scheduled outside imaging windows, with acceleration logged for every well image.
Optional, not standard: a small on-orbit 1 g centrifuge cassette as an in-flight gravity control, like the MVP hardware on the 2020 cardiac flight. This would need a dedicated large bay.
Optional, not standard: optical pH and oxygen sensor spots in the wells, read by the bay microscope, to monitor the sealed HEPES culture.
limitations: LELP-1 runs at most 14 days. The neural-organoid heritage flights lasted about 30 days, so changes seen after a month may be smaller or missing at 14 days. The 3-day cardiac data suggest that early gene changes can be measured.
The standard bay has no in-orbit 1 g centrifuge. Microgravity effects cannot be separated from launch, radiation and hardware effects as cleanly as with the centrifuge control in the ISS MVP.

Mature brain organoids launch live, not frozen, which needs a powered late load and a short pad timeline. We did not find a flight-proven method to cryopreserve whole mature neural organoids and thaw them automatically. The cryopreserved option has flight heritage only for cardiac progenitor spheres, and that thaw was done by hand on the ISS.
There is no crew on board. Bubbles, a blocked line or a leaking well cannot be fixed by hand, so the protocol depends on the automated fluidics working the first time.

The bay has no CO2 supply. The culture relies on HEPES buffering in sealed wells, which limits how long and how dense the culture can be before pH and oxygen drift. Without the optional sensors, pH and oxygen are not measured in flight.
With 24 wells and one organoid per well, groups are small once lines, microglia conditions and time points are split. The heritage authors said their protein data lacked statistical power.
Live-return organoids spend up to about 3 days at 4 C after the flight. Cold storage changes gene expression, so only organoids fixed or RNA-stabilized in orbit give a clean flight end-point.
Electrophysiology (multi-electrode arrays) and single-cell sequencing happen only after return. The bay cannot record neural activity in flight.
Each robotic-arm move raises the g level to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g, so imaging at the central microscope slightly disturbs the microgravity condition.
The BOARDS (Muotri) results quoted here come from ISS National Lab reports. We did not find a peer-reviewed flight paper for them.

corrections_to_leads: The sources we opened for Marotta et al. 2024 (the journal page and the Scripps release) do not name Aspen Neuroscience. The lead that links this flight to Aspen is not supported.

In Marotta et al., the organoids were not cryopreserved for launch. They were shipped at 4 C, flew live in a 37 C CubeLab on SpaceX CRS-19, had no medium exchange for 30 days and came back live. After return, some were plated and some were snap-frozen for RNA sequencing.

The UC San Diego Muotri organoids (BOARDS, UCSD-ORG01) flew on SpaceX CRS-18 (launch planned for July 21, 2019) for about one month, in 2019, not 2019-2020. Their results come from ISS National Lab reports; we found no peer-reviewed flight paper.

The cardiac-sphere lead is confirmed: Rampoldi et al. 2022 (Emory, SpaceX CRS-20, launched March 6, 2020, Techshot MVP). The spheres were cryopreserved progenitor spheres, thawed by hand on board, cultured with medium exchange every other day, fixed in RNAProtect at day 3 and returned live after 22 days.
We could not confirm a liver-organoid flight in the time available, so it is left out.

The lead 'organoids keep growing in sealed culture with media exchange' is only partly right. The neural-organoid flight used sealed vials with no medium exchange; the cardiac flight used medium exchange in the MVP.
Multi-electrode array recordings in Marotta et al. were made only on ground organoids to validate the cryovial method, not on flown organoids.

experiments.title: Protein crystallization for drug formulation
experiments.why: Many drugs are proteins, such as monoclonal antibodies, and today these are usually given by intravenous infusion in hospital. A concentrated, less viscous crystalline suspension could instead be given as an injection under the skin, and better crystals give sharper X-ray structures for drug design. On Earth, sedimentation and convection disturb crystal growth. In microgravity both are reduced, which can give more uniform crystals: on the ISS, Merck got a more uniform, less viscous pembrolizumab suspension, and JAXA got higher-resolution crystals for some proteins.
customers: Biologics formulation teams developing high-concentration antibody suspensions for injection under the skin
Structural biology and drug-discovery labs that need higher-resolution crystal structures of target proteins
Contract research organizations that offer crystallization screening
Academic crystallography groups testing how convection affects crystal quality
Small-molecule polymorph screening, but only for solution processes that work between 4 and 45 C

heritage.mission: Merck pembrolizumab crystallization (CASIS PCG-5) on SpaceX CRS-10, ISS National Lab
heritage.platform: ISS (delivered and returned by SpaceX Dragon)
heritage.what_flew: Batch crystallization of pembrolizumab (Keytruda), 20-40 mg/ml, in 1 ml polysulfone bottles in the Handheld Protein Crystallization Facility. Held at +4 C for 24 h in the MERLIN incubator, then ramped to +30 C. Stayed in MERLIN for 18 days. A ground control with the same protein and reagents ran in parallel on the same temperature schedule.
heritage.finding: Flight suspensions had a single particle size peak at about 39 um. Ground controls had two peaks, at about 13 and 102 um. The flight suspension was less viscous (3.67 vs 5.48 cP at 50 mg/ml). It sedimented in about 57 min, while the ground sample had not fully sedimented after several hours. Dissolved flight crystals kept over 94% binding activity relative to reference pembrolizumab.

heritage.mission: JAXA PCG (high-quality protein crystal growth project)
heritage.platform: ISS (since 2008 in the Protein Crystallization Research Facility on the Kibo module, 293 K / 20 C); samples carried up and down on Progress and Soyuz
heritage.what_flew: Counter-diffusion crystallization: protein in capillaries plugged with agarose gel, inside tubes of crystallization solution in the JAXA Crystallization Box (up to 144 conditions in about 1 litre). 580 proteins crystallized in total. Growth times were six weeks to four months.
heritage.finding: Some space-grown crystals diffracted to higher resolution, for example 1.06 A vs 1.30 A for lipocalin-type prostaglandin D synthase. Success needed a highly homogeneous protein sample and a viscous (PEG) solution. In flights 1 to 5, 40 of 215 samples (19%) gave good results. Return transport was thermally passive. The temperature inside Soyuz sometimes rose above 303 K (30 C), which degraded space-grown crystals, so JAXA added heptadecane phase-change packs (melting at 295 K) and vacuum insulation.

heritage.mission: Varda Space Industries W-1
heritage.year: 2023-2024 (launched 12 June 2023, crystallization started 29 June 2023, landed 21 Feb 2024)
heritage.platform: Free-flyer with a recoverable capsule; landed at the Utah Test and Training Range
heritage.what_flew: In-orbit crystallization of ritonavir, a small-molecule HIV drug and not a protein, from a melt (131 C for 36 min, then 80 C growth for nearly 24 h, then cooled to 15 C). Passive controls of ritonavir Forms I, II, III and amorphous were thermally isolated from the crystallization hardware.
heritage.finding: The returned flight samples were consistent with the metastable Form III of ritonavir. Test samples and passive controls showed excellent stability after return. The results are a ChemRxiv preprint and have not been peer reviewed.

protocol.sample: A purified, highly homogeneous target protein (for example a monoclonal antibody at 20-40 mg/ml, or a protein for X-ray structure work) with a viscous precipitant such as PEG. The conditions are fixed in ground tests before flight.
protocol.container: Large-bay 24-well cassette. 16 sealed batch wells (about 0.5-1 ml each), with protein and precipitant kept in separate reservoirs until the fluidics mix them in orbit. 8 positions hold gel-plugged counter-diffusion capillaries (JAXA style), with the precipitant added by the fluidics at activation.
protocol.launch_state: Live protein solution and precipitant in separate reservoirs, held at 4 C. No crystallization before activation. Not cryopreserved, because freezing would ruin the experiment.
protocol.light_gas: No light needed except for brief microscope imaging. No gas exchange: sealed wells, no CO2 or O2 supply.

steps.action: Late load of the filled cassette at 4 C into the powered bay on the pad. A matching ground-control cassette from the same protein lot is loaded at the same time.
Launch. Bay holds 4 C. Accelerometer and dosimeter logging start.

Arm parked and quiet microgravity confirmed (about 1e-6 g). Baseline brightfield images of all wells. Fluidics mix protein and precipitant in the batch wells and fill the counter-diffusion reservoirs (activation).
Temperature step or ramp to the customer's growth setpoint. Default is 20 C, as in JAXA's PCRF. A warming ramp like Merck's (4 C to 30 C) is also possible, with the ramp rate set by the customer.
Automated brightfield imaging of chosen wells every 6 h to record nucleation time, crystal count and size. Optional fluorescence if the customer adds a trace-labelled protein.
Mid-point check of images on the ground. The customer may change the temperature profile of later wells with a signed command.
Last full imaging pass. Bay set to the customer's return hold temperature. No fixative is added, because crystals stay in their mother liquor.

End of lab operations. Deorbit, reentry and splashdown with the bay still under thermal control. Cassette handed to the courier about 20 min after splashdown in an active thermal shipper at the same setpoint.

sample_return.note: Hold the cassette at the customer's growth or hold temperature (default 20 C, within about +/-2 C) from end of growth to the lab. Do not warm, cool or freeze it unless ground tests show that is safe for that protein. How crystals react to temperature depends on the protein: pembrolizumab crystallized on warming from 4 to 30 C, while JAXA saw space-grown crystals degrade when Soyuz rose above 30 C on return. Handle gently, because crystals sit in liquid and can break under shock. The 72 h limit is our estimate (about 20 min to courier handover plus 1-2 days to the lab) and must be confirmed in ground tests for each protein.

experiments.ground_control: A matching cassette from the same protein lot and solutions, loaded at the same time, runs in a flight-equivalent bay on the ground. Telemetry drives its temperature to replay the flight log, including launch, activation, ramp and return-hold phases. It is activated at the same time by the same type of fluidics. Ideally a launch-vibration profile is applied before activation. Ground and flight samples go to the same lab and are analysed blind with the same methods. A third passive set, never activated, can show what launch and return alone do to the solutions.

Active thermal shipper for the courier at the customer's hold temperature, with a temperature logger
Quiet-period scheduling: no robotic arm motion during nucleation and growth (arm motion raises the level to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g)
Accelerometer data time-stamped and delivered with the images, so the customer can link disturbances to crystal defects
Optional crossed polarizer in the bay microscope to see crystal birefringence (not part of the standard LumaScope-class set-up)
Ground-replay bay for the parallel ground control
limitations: Lab operations last at most 14 days. Merck's samples spent 18 days in the incubator and JAXA growth took six weeks to four months, so LELP-1 suits only fast-growing systems whose conditions are fixed on the ground beforehand.
There is no crew to harvest, mount or flash-cool crystals in orbit. Crystals come back in their mother liquor and can be damaged by reentry and splashdown shocks or by temperature excursions.
There is no X-ray diffraction in flight. Crystal quality is known only after return.
The bay microscope cannot reliably resolve particles of a few microns, so the in-flight size data are qualitative. The full particle size distribution needs ground instruments.
Microgravity helps only some proteins. In JAXA's flights 1 to 5, 40 of 215 samples (19%) gave good results, and success needed highly homogeneous samples in viscous solutions.
Sample volumes are millilitres per well. This is a research and formulation-development service, not drug manufacturing.
The bay range is 4 to 45 C. Melt-based small-molecule processes such as Varda's W-1 ritonavir run (131 C melt, 80 C growth) are out of scope.
Arm motion and any thruster use raise the g-level. Growth wells need quiet periods, and the timeline must be shared with other bays.
LELP-1 is a design in a digital twin. None of this has flown, and all LELP-1 numbers are our estimates.

The paper (Reichert et al., npj Microgravity) appeared in 2019, but the experiment flew in 2017 on SpaceX CRS-10 (19 Feb to 19 Mar 2017) and spent 18 days in the MERLIN incubator on the ISS. Varda W-1 processed ritonavir, a small-molecule HIV drug and not a protein. I could not open a source that states 'Form II was converted to Form III'. experiments.title: Antibiotic resistance of pathogenic bacteria
experiments.why: Drug-resistant bacteria are a large cause of death on Earth: WHO estimates bacterial antimicrobial resistance was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. In spaceflight the problem has a second edge, because dysregulation of the human immune system persists for the duration of a 6-month orbital flight, so an infection that is routine on the ground is harder to treat. Flight data show the bacteria change too, and they do not all change the same way: Salmonella flown on STS-115 had 167 genes differentially expressed and killed mice faster, E. coli grown on the ISS reached a 13-fold higher final cell count than its ground control with smaller cells and thicker envelopes, yet on the EcAMSat free-flyer uropathogenic E. coli came out more susceptible to gentamicin in microgravity, not less. Microgravity is worth using here because it removes sedimentation and buoyancy-driven convection, so each cell sits in a quiet, diffusion-limited layer of its own waste and of the drug, a condition that is hard to hold steady for days on the ground; the disagreement between the flight results so far is the reason to run more of these experiments, not fewer.
customers: Antibiotic developers looking for stress-response targets (sigma-s / rpoS, Hfq) that change drug tolerance without genetic selection
Space agency crew health offices needing dosing evidence for long missions
Academic microbiology and infectious disease labs with modeled-microgravity results that need a real flight test
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and diagnostics companies checking how their assays behave under low shear
Biofilm and medical device companies studying aggregate formation and matrix production
National AMR research programmes funding mechanism work on tolerance and persistence

heritage.mission: STS-115 (Space Shuttle Atlantis)
heritage.what_flew: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium strain chi-3339 in fluid processing apparatus (FPA) units, activated and fixed in flight, with matched ground controls
heritage.finding: 167 genes were differentially expressed in flight versus ground controls (69 up, 98 down) and 73 proteins changed level. The RNA-binding protein Hfq came out as a likely global regulator: expression of 64 genes in the Hfq regulon was altered in flight, 32 percent of the genes identified. Mice infected with the flight bacteria showed decreased time to death, increased mortality across doses and a reduced LD50. Flight samples showed cellular aggregation and clumping associated with the formation of an extracellular matrix.

heritage.mission: E. coli gentamicin culture experiment on the ISS (Zea et al.)
heritage.year: 2017 (paper; the flight year is not stated on the pages we opened)
heritage.platform: ISS, BioServe fluid processing apparatus in a group activation pack inside the CGBA incubator
heritage.what_flew: E. coli ATCC 4157 (non-motile) in Medium E minimal medium with 5 g/L glucose at 30 C, challenged with gentamicin at seven levels from 25 to 175 micrograms/mL in 25 micrograms/mL steps, 49 h total incubation
heritage.finding: A 13-fold increase in final cell count in space with respect to Earth. Space-grown cells were 37 percent of the volume of their matched Earth controls. Cell envelope thickness increased by 25 percent at 25 micrograms/mL and 43 percent at 50 micrograms/mL gentamicin. Outer membrane vesicles were observed on the spaceflight samples but not on the Earth cultures. Note the strain is a laboratory E. coli, not a uropathogen, and the run was at 30 C, not body temperature.

heritage.mission: EcAMSat (E. coli AntiMicrobial Satellite), NASA Ames and Stanford
heritage.platform: 6U free-flying small satellite, 11 kg (a press report at launch gave about 10 kg), carried to the ISS in November 2017 on an Orbital ATK Antares/Cygnus cargo flight and then ejected from the station's Japanese robotic arm into low Earth orbit
heritage.what_flew: Wild-type uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) and its isogenic delta-rpoS mutant, which lacks the sigma factor sigma-s. Both strains were grown to stationary phase in a 48-microwell fluidic card, starved for over 24 h, then dosed with three concentrations of gentamicin. alamarBlue, a redox indicator, was administered and metabolic activity was measured optically using the payload's LED and detector system over a 144 h incubation, with a parallel ground-based control experiment.
heritage.finding: sigma-s is known to increase antibiotic resistance in Earth gravity; EcAMSat tested whether that holds in microgravity. Published result: microgravity did not enhance UPEC resistance to gentamicin - in fact both strains were more susceptible to gentamicin in microgravity. Growth rates of the two strains were unaltered by microgravity, both strains metabolised more slowly in microgravity, and the delta-rpoS mutant was 34 to 37 percent less metabolically active than the wild type across four condition sets (ground with and without gentamicin, microgravity with and without gentamicin). The authors also report that multi-week storage in the payload hardware stressed the cells and may have obscured small differences. Two heritage points for LELP-1: an automated grow-starve-dose-read chain works on an uncrewed free-flyer, and time between loading and dosing has to be kept short.

protocol.sample: Uropathogenic E. coli, BSL-2 clinical isolate, flown as a matched pair: wild type and an isogenic deletion mutant of the stress-response sigma factor gene rpoS. 4 gentamicin levels (0, 25, 55, 100 micrograms/mL) x 2 strains x 3 wells = 24 wells.
protocol.container: One 24-well sealed microfluidic cassette in a large bay, about 400 microlitres per well, each well with its own inlet, outlet and LED/photodiode pair. BSL-2 triple containment with an absorbent secondary tray and a seal pressure sensor.
protocol.launch_state: Live cells, no cryopreservation: loaded at the launch site within 24 h of liftoff and held dormant at 4 C in the sealed wells, with growth medium kept in a separate reservoir and not in contact with the cells. No thaw step and no -80 C cassette. Load-to-dose time is kept to days, because EcAMSat reported that multi-week storage in payload hardware stressed the cells.
protocol.light_gas: No light needed for growth; the only light is the 570 nm and 600 nm LED pairs used for the dye readout, plus the microscope illuminator. No CO2 supply needed: the medium is HEPES-buffered and the sealed air headspace is sized for the well volume. Headspace oxygen is monitored, not replenished.

steps.action: Launch. Bay held at 4 C, cells dormant, seal and pressure logged every minute. Dosimeter running.
Orbit reached and the lab is quiet. Bay ramps to 37 C over 1 h. Pump fills all 24 wells with HEPES-buffered growth medium. Optical density read every 15 min.

Cultures reach stationary phase (expected 18 to 24 h), then are held without fresh medium so they starve, as EcAMSat did for over 24 h before dosing. Microscope takes a brightfield image of every well to check for aggregates before dosing.

Dosing. Gentamicin injected at 0, 25, 55 and 100 micrograms/mL, three wells per strain per level, then alamarBlue redox dye into all 24 wells. Optical readout at 570 and 600 nm every 30 min starts here and runs 72 h. Live/dead fluorescence images every 6 h.
Dose-response window continues. Downlink the optical series once per orbit so the team can confirm the assay is working while there is still time to extend the window.

Robotic arm carries the bay to the central lab for one 40x fluorescence look at the highest-dose wells (aggregates, matrix, vesicle-scale structures). Arm motion window logged, since quasi-steady microgravity is lost to 1e-4 to 1e-3 g while it moves.

End of exposure. 12 wells get RNA stabiliser (transcriptome snapshot taken in orbit), 6 wells get glutaraldehyde fixative for electron microscopy, 6 wells are left live for ground plating. Bay drops to 4 C and holds. Waste line chemically inactivated.
Deorbit, re-entry under the inflatable heat shield, splashdown. Bay stays at 4 C through recovery; samples handed to the customer courier on the recovery ship about 20 min after splashdown.

in_flight.name: Metabolic activity / dose response
in_flight.method: alamarBlue redox dye reduction, read as 570 nm vs 600 nm absorbance by the per-well LED and photodiode pair every 30 min for 72 h. Same readout class EcAMSat flew, where metabolic activity was measured optically using the payload's LED and detector system.

in_flight.name: Growth curve to stationary phase
in_flight.method: Optical density on the same LED/photodiode pair every 15 min from medium fill to dosing.

in_flight.name: Live/dead fraction
in_flight.method: Bay microscope, two fluorescence channels, SYTO 9 and propidium iodide, imaged every 6 h after dosing.

in_flight.name: Aggregation and matrix formation
in_flight.method: Brightfield images of every well before dosing and every 6 h after; one 40x fluorescence session in the central lab on day 5.

in_flight.name: Environment and containment
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure, humidity and seal sensors at 1 min cadence; accelerometer for the arm-motion windows.

in_flight.name: Radiation dose
in_flight.method: Active silicon dosimeter logged through the flight, passive TLDs read after return.

post_flight.name: Viable counts
post_flight.method: CFU plating of the 6 live wells on arrival at the customer lab, plated against the ground control run.

post_flight.name: MIC and MBC confirmation
post_flight.method: Standard broth microdilution on returned isolates, so the flight dye signal is anchored to a clinical susceptibility number.

post_flight.name: Transcriptome
post_flight.method: RNA-seq on the 12 wells stabilised in orbit on day 6, compared with the ground control; targeted at the sigma-s (rpoS) and Hfq regulons.

post_flight.name: Proteome
post_flight.method: LC-MS/MS on the stabilised lysates.

post_flight.name: Cell envelope and ultrastructure
post_flight.method: Transmission electron microscopy on the glutaraldehyde-fixed wells, measuring envelope thickness, cell volume and outer membrane vesicles, as in the ISS E. coli work.

post_flight.name: Genome check
post_flight.method: Whole-genome sequencing of returned isolates to show the change was not a selected mutation.

post_flight.name: Virulence (optional, customer facility)
post_flight.method: Murine infection model on returned live cells, as done for the STS-115 Salmonella. Needs the customer's animal facility and ethics approval; not part of the standard service.

sample_return.note: Fixed and RNA-stabilised wells are robust: 4 C and up to 48 h from day-6 preservation to the lab is fine. The live wells are the tight ones - plate them within 24 h of splashdown, because cells sitting at 4 C in spent medium keep changing expression and losing viability. That is why the transcriptome and electron microscopy samples are preserved in orbit on day 6 rather than on the ship: the only clean snapshot of the flight state is one taken in flight.

experiments.ground_control: An identical cassette in an identical bay inside the flight-spare satellite on the ground, run on a 24 h delayed timeline that replays the actual flight telemetry: measured bay temperature, pressure, humidity and the real fluidics command log, same cell lot, same cassette fill batch, same reagent lots. EcAMSat ran a parallel ground-based control experiment against its flight data, and a second ground-control experiment that showed multi-week storage in the payload hardware stressed the cells - so our ground arm also carries a storage-matched control, and the flight plan keeps load-to-dose time short. Because launch loads, re-entry loads and the 550 km radiation dose are not reproduced on the ground, we also fly a 1 g reference: three wells of each strain in a bay on the onboard centrifuge, so microgravity can be separated from the rest of the flight environment. Without that 1 g arm, any flight-versus-ground difference stays confounded.

Reagent reservoirs: medium 150 mL, 3 gentamicin stocks 10 mL each, alamarBlue 25 mL, RNA stabiliser 30 mL, glutaraldehyde 20 mL, lysis buffer 20 mL
Peristaltic pump and 12-port valve manifold
Triple-containment shell, seals, pressure and humidity sensors
25 W thermoelectric block and heat spreader
Bay controller avionics and harness
Waste bag with chemical inactivation and absorbent secondary tray
Optical readout board: 24 LED/photodiode pairs at 570 and 600 nm

module.basis: Our design estimate, not a flown number. Scaled down from the EcAMSat-class approach - a 48-microwell fluidic card with a redox dye read by an onboard LED and detector system, inside a whole 6U satellite of 11 kg - to a single 24-well cassette in one LELP-1 large bay, where the structure, power, avionics and thermal control of the satellite are already provided. Item masses are design allocations and sum exactly to 5.80 kg, inside the 6.0 kg large-bay limit. Peak power 28 W assumes the 25 W thermoelectric block is software-capped at 23 W during the short windows when the pump (3 W) and the optical board plus controller (2 W) run together, which keeps the bay inside its 30 W limit; at 37 C in a 550 km dawn-dusk orbit the block's steady draw is well below its 25 W maximum, so the cap costs nothing. These numbers need a thermal test on the real cassette before they are more than an estimate.
module.power_peak_w_note: 28 W of a 30 W large-bay limit

needs: Per-well absorbance photometry: 570 nm and 600 nm LED plus photodiode pairs on all 24 wells. The standard bay gives a microscope, not a plate reader, and the redox dye assay is the primary in-flight measurement.
Live/dead fluorescence filter set (SYTO 9 and propidium iodide) on the bay microscope.
A 1 g reference position on the onboard centrifuge for 3 wells of each strain, with the same thermal and fluidic service as the microgravity bay.
Extra reservoirs and lines for RNA stabiliser and glutaraldehyde, and the ability to drop the bay from 37 C to 4 C and hold it there from day 6 through recovery.
Bio-waste bag with chemical inactivation before splashdown, plus a verified seal log for a pathogenic strain under BSL-2 triple containment.
Downlink of the optical series at least once per orbit during the 72 h antibiotic window, so the assay can be confirmed while the mission can still be extended.
Launch-site load of live stationary-phase cells within 24 h of liftoff and a 4 C hold on the pad; this experiment does not use the -80 C cryo path.

A short, controlled load-to-dose interval. EcAMSat found that multi-week storage in the payload hardware stressed the cells and may have hidden small differences, so late load, a short pad hold and early dosing are requirements, not conveniences.
limitations: The flight evidence does not point one way. ISS E. coli grew to a 13-fold higher final cell count in space, while EcAMSat found uropathogenic E. coli more susceptible to gentamicin in microgravity and its growth rate unchanged. One 7-day flight will not settle that; it adds one well-controlled point.
A 2 to 14 day flight gives one dose-response, not evolution. Resistance that arises by selection over weeks of serial passage cannot be studied here.

EcAMSat incubated its cells with the dye for 144 h after dosing. Our 7-day baseline gives a 72 h window; matching EcAMSat's readout length needs a 10-day mission, which is inside the 2 to 14 day envelope but costs more.

No crew. There is no plating, no colony picking, no re-dosing decision in the moment and no fixing a stuck valve. Every move must be in the fluidic plan before launch, and a single pump or valve failure can cost the whole bay.

24 wells means 3 replicates per condition. That resolves a large shift in tolerance, not a small one. EcAMSat's own report notes that cell stress in the hardware could obscure small differential effects, so customers wanting statistical power should buy more than one bay.

The in-flight readout is dye reduction, that is metabolic activity, not colony-forming units. A clinical MIC number must be confirmed on the ground, and returned live cells spend 1 to 2 days at 4 C before plating.
Only wells preserved in orbit give a clean flight-state transcriptome or ultrastructure. Anything judged after the courier hand-off has a day or two of cold storage written into it.

Launch loads, re-entry loads and the 550 km radiation dose are confounders. Only the onboard 1 g control separates microgravity from them, and that control shares the same radiation and vibration history, not the same gravity history as a laboratory on Earth.

Quasi-steady microgravity is about 1e-6 g near the centre of mass, but rises to 1e-4 to 1e-3 g while the robotic arm moves. Data taken in those windows is not a clean microgravity measurement and is flagged as such.
No animal virulence test on board. The STS-115 result that flight Salmonella killed mice faster needed returned live cells and a ground animal facility; LELP-1 can return the cells, nothing more.
No host. There is no infection model, no human pharmacokinetics and no immune system in the bay, so nothing here translates directly into a dosing recommendation for a crew member.
No CO2 supply. Fine for E. coli, but a bacteria-plus-host-cell co-culture would need HEPES-buffered media and gas-permeable lids and is a harder sell in a sealed bay.
LELP-1 is a design in a digital twin. No bay, cassette or thermoelectric block described here has flown, and every mass, power and timing number above is our estimate awaiting test.

corrections_to_leads: The biggest correction. The previous draft said EcAMSat's published result could not be quoted and presented the mission as supporting a 'space makes bacteria more resistant' story. The abstract of Padgen et al. 2020 is served by the Europe PMC REST API and we opened it. The published result is the opposite: 'micro-g did not enhance UPEC resistance to Gm; in fact, both strains were more susceptible to Gm in micro-g.' Growth rates of both strains were unaltered by microgravity, both metabolised more slowly in microgravity, and the delta-rpoS mutant was 34 to 37 percent less metabolically active than the wild type across four condition sets. The entry now states this, and the page frames the field as unsettled rather than one-directional.

The claim that 'uropathogenic E. coli becomes more resistant to gentamicin under modeled microgravity and the increase is controlled by sigma-s' is not in the body of any page we opened; it appears in search-result text. What Padgen's abstract says is that sigma-s has been shown to increase antibiotic resistance in Earth gravity and that it was unknown whether this holds in microgravity. We now say that instead.

EcAMSat mass: Padgen et al. call it 'an 11-kg small satellite'. The 'about 10 kg' figure comes from a launch-day press report (23 pounds). We use 11 kg from the flight paper and note the press figure. 6U is confirmed by the NASA page title, and the 48-well fluidic card by both the NASA NTRS payload record and the press report.

Reference URL fixed. The draft cited Padgen et al. with a PubMed search query URL (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=EcAMSat), which is a search page, not a record. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31987476/ returns a cookie wall, europepmc.org/article/MED/31987476 returns 403 and doi.org redirects to a paywalled Elsevier page. The reference now points at the Europe PMC REST record we actually opened, with the DOI and PMID in the citation text.

EcAMSat's ground control was described as 'an identical satellite in the lab'. Nothing we opened says that. Padgen's abstract says 'a parallel ground-based control experiment' plus 'a second ground-control experiment'. Corrected.

New and useful: Padgen reports that multi-week storage in the payload hardware stressed the cells and may have obscured small differences between strains and between flight and ground. That is a direct design constraint for us, so late loading, a short pad hold, early dosing and a storage-matched ground arm are now written into the protocol, needs and ground control.

Zea et al. 2017 envelope thickness was given as a range, '25 to 43 percent'. The paper gives two dose-specific values: 25 percent at 25 micrograms/mL and 43 percent at 50 micrograms/mL gentamicin. Corrected.

Removed: 'E. coli cultured on ISS grew in gentamicin levels that normally inhibit it'. The opened Zea page does not say that. What it does say - 13-fold higher final cell count, cells at 37 percent of control volume, thicker envelope, outer membrane vesicles only in flight - is what we now state. Also kept the earlier caveat that this was E. coli ATCC 4157 at 30 C, not a clinical uropathogen at body temperature.

Confirmed unchanged: Wilson et al. PNAS 2007, STS-115 on Space Shuttle Atlantis, September 2006, Salmonella Typhimurium chi-3339, 104(41):16299-16304. All of 167 / 69 up / 98 down / 73 proteins / 64 Hfq-regulon genes check out on the PMC page, and the virulence increase was measured in a murine model (decreased time to death, reduced LD50), not inferred from expression alone.

Earth-side burden figure confirmed from the WHO fact sheet we opened: bacterial AMR associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. We still could not reach the Lancet GBD AMR paper, so the 1.27 million attributable figure for 2019 is not used.

Added an agency source for the EcAMSat payload (NASA NTRS record 20190001420, a 2016 preprint by Matin and colleagues) so the hardware facts rest on NASA documents rather than press reporting. It is cited as a preprint describing payload and protocol, not as the results paper. This takes the list to 8 references, one above the suggested 7, because the EcAMSat facts split across a NASA results page, the published paper, the payload preprint and a launch report.

Module and protocol arithmetic re-checked and unchanged: items sum to exactly 5.80 kg against the 6.0 kg large-bay limit, peak power 28 W against 30 W, and the stated 23 + 3 + 2 W breakdown also sums to 28 W. The launch-state wording was simplified, because loading stationary-phase cells and then growing them to stationary phase again in orbit read as a contradiction; the flight plan is live cells held dormant at 4 C, grown on day 1, starved, then dosed on day 3, which matches EcAMSat's 'starvation for over 24 h' before gentamicin.

verification.notes:
All eight reference URLs were opened and read in this session. Seven of the original references survived; one URL (Padgen et al.) was replaced because it pointed at a PubMed search query rather than a record, and one agency reference (NASA NTRS 20190001420) was added so the EcAMSat hardware facts rest on NASA documents instead of press reporting. That puts the list at 8, one above the suggested maximum; drop r5 (Spaceflight Now) if a hard cap of 7 matters, at the cost of the launch-and-deployment detail, which no other opened page carries.

The one serious error was the EcAMSat heritage item. The previous agent concluded the Padgen 2020 full text was unreachable and therefore quoted no result, then framed the mission as carrying a resistance-increases hypothesis to orbit. The abstract is in fact served by the Europe PMC REST API, and the published result is the reverse: microgravity did not enhance resistance and both strains were more susceptible to gentamicin in microgravity. That changes the honest framing of the whole entry, so the why-section, the heritage finding and the limitations now present the flight literature as contradictory - ISS E. coli grew far more, EcAMSat UPEC became more susceptible - which is a stronger and truer sales argument for flying the experiment than a one-directional story would have been.

Two smaller fabrication-adjacent problems were fixed: the "modeled microgravity plus sigma-s" mechanism sentence came from search-result text, not from any page body, and the claim that ISS E. coli "grew in gentamicin levels that normally inhibit it" is not on the Zea page. Both were replaced with sourced statements. The EcAMSat ground control was also overstated as "an identical satellite in the lab"; the paper says a parallel ground-based control experiment.

One genuinely useful new fact came out of the check and is now in the design: Padgen reports that multi-week storage in the payload hardware stressed the cells and may have masked small effects. Short load-to-dose time and a storage-matched ground arm are now explicit requirements.

Still open, and worth a later pass: the Padgen full text is paywalled (Elsevier 403), so the entry quotes the abstract only - buying the paper would let you add per-dose numbers. The flight year of the Zea et al. ISS run is not stated on the pages we opened, so the heritage item says so rather than guessing. EcAMSat deployment from the Japanese module arm rests on a pre-deployment press report describing the plan; a post-deployment agency confirmation would be better. Protocol, mass and power all pass plausibility and the bay limits; they remain our estimate.

experiments.title: Seed germination and root growth
experiments.why: Every crop-growing system for long missions starts with a seed that must sprout, find its way and form a working root. On Earth, gravity tells roots which way to grow, so it is hard to see what other cues (light, touch, internal programs) do on their own. In microgravity that cue is removed, so researchers can see how roots orient, skew and wave without gravity and which genes change. The same early-seedling data also helps breeders and agencies screen seed lines before they commit them to longer crop experiments.
customers: Space agency plant and life-support programmes (for example ISRO, NASA, ESA crop and bioregenerative life-support teams)
University plant biology labs studying gravitropism, phototropism and root growth
Seed and agri-biotech companies screening varieties or reporter lines for space farming
Nutrition and food researchers looking at sprouts as fresh food for crews
Student and early-career research teams needing a short, automated plant flight

heritage.mission: CROPS-1 (Compact Research Module for Orbital Plant Studies) on PSLV-C60 POEM-4
heritage.platform: PSLV orbital experiment module (POEM-4), about 350 km orbit
heritage.what_flew: Eight cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) seeds, two per chamber in four chambers, in a closed box with active thermal control. It had porous clay soil pellets with slow-release fertiliser, four warm and four cool LEDs on 16 h / 8 h, a camera, and CO2/O2, pressure, temperature, humidity and soil-moisture sensors. Built by ISRO.
heritage.finding: Water was injected into the soil by a valve commanded from the ground. Seeds sprouted on day 4 and two leaves were visible on day 5. This showed germination and growth to the two-leaf stage in an automated box on an orbital platform.

heritage.mission: ABRS Arabidopsis root imaging (Paul, Amalfitano and Ferl)
heritage.platform: International Space Station, Advanced Biological Research System (ABRS) with GFP Imaging System
heritage.what_flew: Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings (cultivars WS and Col-0) on phytagel nutrient gel in 100 mm square Petri plates with directional light. Photos every six hours for the 15 days of the experiment. Samples preserved in RNAlater.
heritage.finding: Root skewing and waving, thought to need gravity, still occurred in spaceflight. WS skewed strongly to the right in orbit, while Col-0 showed little deviation. Roots grew away from the light.

heritage.mission: TROPI (Tropisms)
heritage.year: 2006 (STS-121, July 2006; more hardware on STS-115, Sept 2006)
heritage.platform: International Space Station, European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS) with two centrifuge rotors (0-2 g)
heritage.what_flew: Arabidopsis seed cassettes on nutrient-soaked filter paper, hydrated in orbit and grown under light at set g-levels. Recorded on video. Frozen at -80 C on day 5 and returned in cold stowage on STS-116, STS-117 and STS-120.
heritage.finding: Gene analysis showed plant hormone pathways (auxin, cytokinin, ethylene, brassinosteroids) were affected by microgravity. Software problems compromised video collection. NASA reported the root and shoot light-response analysis as ongoing.

heritage.mission: Seedling Growth-2 (SG2)
heritage.year: 2014 (launched on SpaceX CRS-4, September 2014; returned on CRS-5, February 2015)
heritage.platform: International Space Station, European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS)
heritage.what_flew: Arabidopsis thaliana (Landsberg erecta) seeds hydrated in orbit and grown for six days: 96 h of white light, then 48 h of one-sided blue light. Grown in microgravity and at several centrifuge g-levels up to 1 g. Seedlings were frozen at -80 C in the ISS GLACIER freezer and returned frozen.
heritage.finding: RNA-seq showed gene expression that depended on the g-level. Microgravity samples were enriched in photosynthesis genes. The authors suggest that root blue-light phototropism may reduce the gravitational stress response.

heritage.mission: Axiom-4, Indian experiment 'Sprouting of methi & moong seeds with relevance to crew nutrition'
heritage.year: 2025 (ISRO gave the undocking from the ISS as scheduled for 14 July 2025)
heritage.what_flew: Fenugreek (methi) and green gram (moong) seeds for a sprouting study aimed at crew nutrition.
heritage.finding: ISRO reported the experiment as completed and being readied for return to Earth for analysis. We did not find peer-reviewed results, so no outcome is claimed here.

protocol.sample: Dry seeds of Arabidopsis thaliana (for example Col-0 and WS, or a GFP reporter line), about 20 seeds per plate. A large-seed crop such as cowpea or moong can replace one plate.
protocol.container: Four sealed square seed plates (about 100 mm, nutrient gel or germination membrane) with gas-permeable covers. They are held upright in a fixed orientation in the large-bay cassette frame. Each plate is plumbed to the bay fluidics for hydration and fixation.
protocol.launch_state: Dry, dormant seeds (not hydrated), dark, bay at 18-22 C
protocol.light_gas: White LEDs 16 h on / 8 h off (the photoperiod CROPS used). From day 4, one-sided blue LED light on half the plates for the phototropism test. Dim green or IR light only for imaging in the dark period. No CO2 supply: the bay is sealed with launch air (CROPS started at 20.9% O2 and 400-600 ppm CO2), and O2/CO2 are logged. Seedling biomass at this stage is small.

steps.action: Ground: load dry seeds on plates, seal bay, integrate. Split the same seed lot into a ground control and an unflown dry-seed archive.

After orbit checkout: image dry plates, bring bay to 22 C, and hydrate each plate with dilute nutrient solution from the fluidics reservoir. Start white LED 16 h / 8 h and time-lapse imaging every 6 h.
Score germination (radicle emergence) from images. Add water only if sensors show plates drying.
Switch two plates to one-sided blue light (phototropism test). Two plates stay on white light. Keep the robotic arm idle during this window if possible.
Fluorescence imaging of reporter-line plates (if flown) and final morphology image set.
Fix in flight: flood two plates with RNA-stabilising fixative (RNAlater-type, for gene expression) and two with an aldehyde fixative (for microscopy). Image after fixation, then set bay to 4 C.
Hold at 4 C with lights off until re-entry (any day up to day 14). Hand to the customer's courier on the recovery ship.

in_flight.name: Germination rate and timing
in_flight.method: Time-lapse macro images every 6 h; count radicle emergence per plate

in_flight.name: Root length, growth rate, root angle, skewing and waving
in_flight.method: Image analysis of the time-lapse series (root tracing), as in the ABRS study

in_flight.name: Phototropic bending of roots and hypocotyls
in_flight.method: Images before and after one-sided blue light, compared with white-light plates

in_flight.name: Reporter gene expression (optional)
in_flight.method: Fluorescence channel of the bay microscope or the central 40x microscope, for GFP reporter lines

in_flight.name: Growth environment
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, humidity, pressure, O2/CO2 logging, acceleration sensor and dosimeter (active silicon + passive TLD)

post_flight.name: Gene expression
post_flight.method: RNA extraction from RNA-stabilised seedlings, RNA-seq against ground controls

post_flight.name: Root cell structure
post_flight.method: Confocal microscopy of fixed roots stained for cell walls (for example calcofluor white, as in Paul et al. 2012)

post_flight.name: Final morphology
post_flight.method: High-resolution scans of fixed plates: root length, angle, root hair and lateral root counts

post_flight.name: Seed viability and radiation effects
post_flight.method: Germination test of unhydrated flown seeds against archive seeds; passive TLD dose readout

sample_return.note: Samples are fixed in orbit, so they do not need to be alive at return. Keep fixed plates at 4 C from fixation (day 7) to the lab. 336 h covers the time from fixation to re-entry on day 14, plus courier time. This limit is our estimate; check it against the fixative maker's storage data. Live seedlings returned unfixed would no longer reflect the microgravity state after landing.

experiments.ground_control: An identical flight-spare module on the ground, loaded from the same seed lot on the same day. It runs the same hydration, light, imaging and fixation timeline at 1 g with plates held vertical, and replays the logged flight temperature, humidity and light record about 1-2 days behind the flight. An unflown dry-seed archive kept at matched temperature separates storage and launch effects from germination effects. A clinostat or random positioning machine run can be added as a simulated-microgravity reference, but it does not replace flight.

items.item: Four sealed seed plates with gas-permeable covers and frame
LED panel (white + one-sided blue + green/IR imaging light) with driver
Two macro cameras with fixed optics (whole-plate time-lapse)
Fluidics: nutrient reservoir, two fixative reservoirs, micro-pumps, valves, lines
O2/CO2 and humidity sensor pack
Module controller and data storage board
Structure, inner containment layer, harness

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source claim. We chose the large bay because whole seedling plates, a light panel and macro cameras do not fit the medium cassette. Mass is scaled from small-satellite hardware classes and leaves 0.5 kg of margin under the 6.0 kg limit. Peak power: LEDs about 10 W, cameras 4 W, pumps 3 W, controller 3 W, sensors 2 W = 22 W, under the 30 W bay limit. The bay's own 25 W thermoelectric block is a bay service and is not counted here.

needs: LED lighting panel inside the bay (white for growth, one-sided blue for phototropism, green/IR for imaging in the dark period)
Macro camera(s) imaging whole plates; the standard inverted cell microscope cannot image seedling morphology
O2/CO2 sensing in the sealed bay air
Fluidics plumbed to each plate for in-orbit hydration and two different fixatives
Fixed plate orientation relative to the light source and known orientation to the satellite axes
A quiet window with the robotic arm idle during the phototropism and imaging phase (arm motion raises acceleration to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g)
Hold at 4 C after fixation through re-entry and recovery
limitations: 2-14 days covers germination and early seedlings only (up to about the two-leaf stage in crops like cowpea). No flowering, seed-to-seed cycles or crop yield studies.
No in-flight 1 g centrifuge, unlike the EMCS on the ISS. Flight and ground differences therefore mix microgravity with launch, radiation and hardware effects.
No -80 C freezer for return. Samples are chemically fixed at 4 C, which suits RNA and microscopy but limits some assays (for example, metabolites or enzyme activity may need frozen tissue).
Fixing in flight is not proven for this layout. In microgravity, fixative may not cover gel-grown seedlings evenly. Fixative delivery must be tested on the ground and in a flight-like setup first.
No crew: plates cannot be swapped, re-wet by hand, or rescued if seeds fail to hydrate. Water behaves differently in microgravity and can bead or bubble.
Sealed bay air with no CO2 supply limits plant number and growth stage. Larger seedlings or many seeds would change O2/CO2 levels.
In flight, imaging covers whole plates only. Detailed cell-level root data comes only after return.
A 550 km sun-synchronous orbit has a different radiation environment from the ISS. Log the dose and compare it before pooling results with ISS data.
Any live material after landing has sensed gravity again during the 1-2 day trip. Only samples fixed in flight reflect the microgravity state.

corrections_to_leads: CROPS: the ISRO CROPS page says seeds sprouted on day 4 and two leaves were visible on day 5 (eight cowpea seeds). It flew on POEM-4 at about 350 km. ISRO's PSLV launch list gives the PSLV-C60 launch as 30 December 2024. The POEM-4 payload page shows 22 December 2024 only as its page date, not as a launch date. The page does not name VSSC, so the builder is given as ISRO.

Paul et al. 2012 is confirmed: Paul AL, Amalfitano CE, Ferl RJ, BMC Plant Biology 12:232. The hardware was ABRS on the ISS, delivered on STS-130 in February 2010, with photos every 6 h for 15 days. The finding is that skewing and waving still happen without gravity, with cultivar differences (WS skews right, Col-0 shows little deviation).
TROPI: NASA reports that video collection was compromised by software problems, and that the root/shoot light-response analysis was ongoing. Only the gene-pathway finding is stated as a result.

Axiom-4 (2025): the ISRO page names the experiment 'Sprouting of methi & moong seeds with relevance to crew nutrition' and says only that it was completed and being readied for return. It gives undocking as scheduled for 14 July 2025. We found no peer-reviewed results. A claim on a coaching website that moong germinated 18% faster was not from a primary source and was not used.

experiments.title: Alloy solidification
experiments.why: Most metal parts start as a liquid that freezes in a mould. The grain structure that forms then sets their strength, so casting and welding models need clean data on how grains grow. On Earth, buoyancy-driven flow and the settling or floating of crystals in the melt mix up that picture. In microgravity, melt flow and sedimentation are suppressed and solute moves mainly by diffusion, so growth can be compared more directly with theory and simulations.
customers: Aluminium casting and alloy producers (automotive, aerospace) who use solidification models to set process windows
Suppliers of grain refiners who need clean data on how equiaxed grains start and grow
University and institute solidification groups that test phase-field, front-tracking and CAFE models
Software vendors who validate casting and welding simulation codes
Space agency materials science programmes that want more flight opportunities between ISS increments

heritage.mission: CETSOL (ESA MAP project), Materials Science Laboratory
heritage.what_flew: Hypo-eutectic Al-7 wt.% Si alloys, with and without grain refiners, solidified under different temperature gradients and cooling conditions
heritage.finding: Non-refined alloys grew purely columnar. The columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET) appeared only in refined alloys. It was sharp when the solidification velocity rose suddenly, and progressive when the temperature gradient fell steadily. Temperature and grain-structure data gave critical values of position, gradient and velocity at the CET for model testing.

heritage.mission: DECLIC-DSI (Directional Solidification Insert of DECLIC)
heritage.what_flew: Transparent succinonitrile-0.24 wt% camphor alloy in a cylindrical crucible with a 10 mm inner diameter, directionally solidified at 1.5 and 2.0 um/s in a 19 K/cm gradient, with in situ optical observation of the interface
heritage.finding: Single cells or rows of cells from one grain can invade a neighbouring grain with a different misorientation, so grain boundaries take convoluted shapes. Phase-field simulations reproduced the invasion.

heritage.mission: XRMON-GF on MASER 12
heritage.platform: Sounding rocket (launched 13 February 2012 from Esrange, Sweden)
heritage.what_flew: Gradient furnace with in situ X-ray radiography, directional solidification of an Al-20 wt% Cu sample
heritage.finding: This was the first directional solidification experiment with in situ X-ray radiography in microgravity, where transport by diffusion dominates. It used about six minutes of microgravity. The authors say the results confirm the value of in situ observation for studying how the microstructure changes during solidification.

heritage.mission: SJ-10 (Shijian-10) materials science programme
heritage.platform: Recoverable scientific experiment satellite (return capsule recovered after 12 days in orbit)
heritage.what_flew: Melt-growth and wetting experiments: compound semiconductors (InAsSb, InGaSb) and Bi2Te3-based alloys, plus wetting of metal alloys including Sn-based alloys
heritage.finding: InAsSb grew detached from the crucible wall in orbit, but touched the wall in the ground run. With buoyancy convection suppressed, composition was more uniform in InGaSb and Bi2Te3-based samples. Interfacial reaction played a significant role in how the interface of the Sn-based alloys changed.

protocol.sample: Transparent model alloy: succinonitrile (SCN) with a small camphor addition (for example 0.24 wt% camphor, the DECLIC-DSI composition), degassed, filled under vacuum and sealed on the ground. Option: a second crucible with a different solute content.
protocol.container: Sealed glass or quartz cylindrical crucible, about 10 mm inner diameter and about 100 mm long, with thermocouples along the wall. It sits in a miniature Bridgman stage (hot zone plus cold zone with a translation stage) inside a large-bay containment shell.
protocol.launch_state: Solid alloy sample at bay temperature (SCN melts near 57 C, so it stays solid at a 20 C launch setpoint)
protocol.light_gas: No gas exchange: the crucible is sealed. Transmitted LED light is on only while images are taken. The hot zone runs at about 70 C and the cold zone at about 30 C, giving roughly 19 K/cm across the interface (our estimate, sized to match DECLIC-DSI). The 70 C hot zone is above the 45 C limit of the standard bay block, so the module needs its own insulated heater (see needs).

steps.action: Launch with the sample solid. Bay block holds 20 C. Module unpowered except housekeeping sensors.

After satellite commissioning, ground confirms an arm-quiet window. Bay block set to 30 C (cold-zone sink). Hot-zone heater ramps to 70 C. Part of the sample melts and the interface settles in the gradient. Hold 24 h so solute spreads out by diffusion. Reference images every 10 min.
Run 1: pull at 1.5 um/s for about 6 h (about 30 mm). Images every 1 to 2 min, thermocouple and accelerometer logs at 1 Hz. The arm stays parked.
Move the crucible back to remelt the grown part. Hold 24 h to homogenise again. Downlink a reduced image set for the ground team to check.
Run 2: pull at 2.0 um/s for about 5 h. Same imaging.
Remelt and hold 24 h.

Run 3: step change in velocity during the run (for example 1.5 to 2.0 um/s) to watch the cell pattern change and grain competition. Ground may change the velocities for runs 3 and 4 based on runs 1 and 2 (signed command checked by the mission guardian).
Remelt and hold 24 h.
Run 4: repeat run 1 to check reproducibility, or a slower velocity chosen by the science team.
Final directional solidification of the whole sample at a low velocity so all of it is solid. Turn off the hot zone. Bay block brings the sample to 15 C.
Hold at 15 C through de-orbit, re-entry and splashdown. Full image archive kept on board as a backup to the downlinked set.

in_flight.name: Solid-liquid interface pattern (cell and dendrite spacing, cell shape, grain boundaries, cell invasion between grains)
in_flight.method: Dedicated camera with long-working-distance optics and transmitted LED light, looking along the growth axis. This is not the standard inverted cell microscope.

in_flight.name: Temperature field and gradient at the interface
in_flight.method: Thermocouples along the crucible plus hot-zone and cold-zone control sensors

in_flight.name: Growth velocity and interface position
in_flight.method: Translation-stage encoder compared with interface position tracked in the images

in_flight.name: Residual acceleration during each run
in_flight.method: Bay accelerometer, logged so each image can be matched to the g-level (quasi-steady about 1e-6 g; runs flagged if the arm moved)

in_flight.name: Containment and module health
in_flight.method: Bay pressure and seal sensors, heater current and module housekeeping

post_flight.name: Final frozen pattern in the last solidified section
post_flight.method: Optical microscopy of the intact crucible in the customer's lab, compared with the last in-flight images

post_flight.name: Comparison with models
post_flight.method: Phase-field or other simulations using the logged velocity, gradient and g-level history

post_flight.name: Ground reference runs
post_flight.method: The same module design and sample batch run on Earth with gravity along and against the growth direction (see ground control)

post_flight.name: For the metallic-alloy furnace option only: grain structure, columnar-to-equiaxed position, segregation
post_flight.method: Sectioning and metallography, EBSD grain orientation mapping, and composition analysis of the returned Al-Si or Al-Cu rods

sample_return.note: Most of the science is in the downlinked images, so return is not urgent. Keep the transparent alloy well below its melting range (pure SCN melts near 57 C) so the final pattern stays frozen. 4 to 25 C is fine. Avoid mechanical shock to the glass crucible. Solid metallic samples from the furnace option have no temperature limit once they cool.

experiments.ground_control: An identical flight-spare module with crucibles filled from the same alloy batch runs the same timeline (same gradients, velocities and hold times) in the customer's lab or ours. It runs once with gravity along the growth direction and once against it, so convection effects can be separated from the microgravity result. Thermal and imaging settings are copied from the flight log. Published ISS DECLIC-DSI results on SCN-camphor serve as an outside benchmark.

items.item: Sealed glass crucible with SCN-camphor sample and wall thermocouples
Hot-zone heater block and cold-zone copper block tied to the bay thermoelectric block
Linear translation stage with stepper motor and encoder
Imaging: CMOS camera, long-working-distance optics, LED transmitted light
Insulation (aerogel and multilayer) and structural frame
Electronics: heater driver, motor driver, thermocouple readout, controller and storage
Containment interface plate, seals and harness

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source claim. It is sized after the DECLIC-DSI transparent-alloy runs (10 mm crucible, 19 K/cm, 1.5 to 2.0 um/s). Peak power: hot-zone heat-up about 15 W, motor 3 W, camera and LED 4 W, electronics 4 W, total about 26 W. Steady power during a run is about 15 W. This fits the large bay's 6.0 kg and 30 W. The bay's own block works only as the cold-zone sink at 30 C. Metallic alloys are not possible in this module: see needs and limitations for the separate furnace-bay option.

needs: Internal hot zone at about 70 C, above the 45 C limit of the standard bay block. The module needs its own insulated heater, with an approved thermal interface so neighbouring bays stay within their setpoints.
Axial imaging camera, transmitted LED light and a translation stage. The standard inverted cell microscope cannot image a directional-solidification interface along the growth axis.
Downlink for about 1 to 3 GB of images over the mission (our estimate), plus on-board storage for the full archive.
Arm-quiet windows: no robotic arm motion during growth runs, because arm motion raises acceleration to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g. Scheduled through the mission guardian.
Bay temperature kept below about 35 C during re-entry and recovery (our estimate, a margin below the alloy's melting range) so the final frozen pattern is preserved.

Metallic alloys (Al-Si, Al-Cu) need a separate furnace bay variant (our proposal, our estimates): a gradient furnace with a hot zone of about 700 to 800 C, taking two large-bay slots (about 12 kg). It would draw about 200 W during the 2 to 4 h melt-back and about 100 to 150 W during solidification, about 1 to 1.5 kWh per run. That is several times the 30 W bay limit, so it needs its own power line and power scheduling against the 600 W array and 1.5 kWh battery (feasible in the near-continuously sunlit dawn-dusk orbit at one run per day). It would also need a sealed high-temperature cartridge, radiative heat rejection to the bus, and quench capability. Each run would process 1 to 3 rods about 8 mm by 100 mm. For comparison, the ISS Materials Science Research Rack processes sample cartridges at up to 1400 C.
limitations: A standard bay cannot melt metal. Al-based alloys need furnace temperatures of several hundred C and power far above 30 W. The standard offer is limited to transparent organic model alloys, which melt near 57 C and still need a module heater above the 45 C bay limit.
No in situ X-ray radiography of metals. XRMON-type X-ray imaging needs a source, detector and power well beyond a bay. Metal samples in the furnace option would be studied only after return.
Sample size is small (about 10 mm by 100 mm, our estimate). Long rods and multi-sample cartridges like those processed in ISS rack furnaces are not possible.

No crew. Crucibles cannot be swapped, refilled or re-aligned. A bubble or a stuck stage cannot be fixed, and the number of runs is limited to what one sealed crucible allows (about 4 to 5 remelt-and-grow cycles in 10 days).
Lab operations last at most 14 days. Very slow growth or diffusion-limited holds that take weeks cannot be done.
Arm motion raises acceleration to 1e-4 to 1e-3 g, so runs must be scheduled around robotic operations. Customers with other bays may need to accept arm-free windows.
Downlink bandwidth limits image rate and resolution. The full high-rate data is only available after recovery.
The metallic furnace bay is a proposal, not a current LELP-1 service. It would take two large-bay slots and a share of satellite power during each run, which affects the rest of the mission plan.

experiments.title: Bioreactor for tissue engineering and biomanufacturing
experiments.why: Engineered tissues such as cartilage and heart muscle are hard to grow on Earth. Thick 3D constructs starve in the middle, and gravity makes cells and soft gels settle. In microgravity there is no sedimentation and no buoyant convection, so a perfusion bioreactor must deliver nutrients and oxygen by pumped flow alone. This lets researchers separate the effects of gravity, flow and shear on tissue growth. Flight results so far show that gravity matters: cartilage grown on Mir came back smaller and mechanically weaker, and engineered heart tissues on the ISS lost contractile force. That makes space a test bed for tissue-engineering methods, disease models and ideas for in-space biomanufacturing.

Organ-on-chip and heart-on-chip developers validating automated platforms
Pharmaceutical companies using engineered tissues for cardiac safety and disease models
University tissue-engineering and stem-cell labs
