heritage.mission: Mir tissue-engineered cartilage experiment (hardware up on STS-79, back on STS-81)
heritage.what_flew: Bovine articular chondrocytes on polyglycolic acid scaffold discs, grown 3 months on Earth and then 4 more months on Mir at 37 C in the Biotechnology System (BTS): a rotating, perfused bioreactor with a 125 ml annular space, peristaltic pump and silicone membrane gas exchanger fed with 10% CO2 in air, with pH and pO2 monitoring. Matched constructs stayed on Earth at 1 g.
heritage.finding: Both groups made viable cartilage with proteoglycan and type II collagen. The Mir constructs were more spherical, smaller and mechanically inferior, with about 3-fold lower aggregate modulus (0.31 vs 0.93 MPa) than the Earth constructs.

heritage.mission: Cell Science-Validation (CS-V), NASA Bioculture System, SpaceX-13
heritage.what_flew: Bioculture System with 10 independently controlled cassettes. Each cassette has a perfusion bioreactor based on porous hollow fibers, computer-controlled fluidics, and its own temperature and flow-rate control. It was validated with mouse MLO-Y4 cells and human iPS-derived cardiomyocytes. Later flights: CS-02 on SpaceX-18 (2019) and CS-04 on SpaceX-22 (2021).
heritage.finding: The system was validated on the ISS. It provides independent temperature and flow control for each cassette and shear-free perfusion culture with automated or manual operation.

heritage.mission: Heart-on-a-chip engineered heart tissues, SpaceX CRS-20
heritage.what_flew: Engineered human heart tissues made from iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes in an automated heart-on-a-chip platform. Magnets in flexible posts were read by magnetic sensors to track force. The tissues were kept at 37 C and 5% CO2 in the Space Automated Bioproduct Laboratory incubator for about 30 days. Crew exchanged medium and preserved tissues at 12, 19 and 26 days after launch. There were 20 flight tissues and 16 ground tissues; the ground tissues ran on the same timeline at 1 g.
heritage.finding: Flight tissues showed lower twitch force, more irregular beating, shorter sarcomeres and mitochondrial damage. Genes for contraction went down, and pathways linked to oxidative stress, inflammation and heart failure went up. The beat irregularity went away after return to Earth, but the force deficit was still there 9 days after return.

protocol.sample: Pre-formed 3D engineered tissue constructs, for example chondrocyte-seeded porous scaffold discs or iPSC-cardiomyocyte tissues. 2 constructs in each of 4 independent perfusion chambers (8 constructs per bay), all from one batch shared with the ground control.
protocol.container: Large-bay perfusion module: 4 sealed perfusion chambers on a closed-loop flow path, a medium reservoir, a waste bag, fixative, RNA-stabilizer and rinse reservoirs, a silicone membrane gas exchanger with a bubble trap, in-line pH, dissolved-oxygen and glucose/lactate sensors, a camera, and a small thermoelectric cold pad under each chamber plus an insulated pocket for medium aliquots, so fixed chambers can be held at 4 C inside the 37 C bay.
protocol.launch_state: Live constructs, matured on the ground, in HEPES-buffered medium at 37 C; late-loaded about 48 h or less before launch with the bay powered
protocol.light_gas: Dark except short LED pulses for imaging. No CO2 supply, so the medium is HEPES-buffered. Oxygen reaches the medium from the sealed bay air through the membrane gas exchanger. pH and dissolved oxygen are logged continuously.

steps.action: Load constructs into the 4 chambers, prime medium, seal bay, start 37 C hold and slow perfusion; late load into LELP-1.
Launch. Perfusion paused or at minimum flow during ascent; temperature, pressure and acceleration logged.
After orbit checkout: start nominal intermittent perfusion, take baseline images of every construct, log pH, dissolved oxygen, glucose and lactate.
Early time point: chamber A is valved off, drained and filled with 4% paraformaldehyde. After 24 h it is flushed with buffer and its cold pad cools it to 4 C.
Days 3-6: daily partial exchange of fresh medium; spent-medium aliquot to the cold pocket; imaging every 6 h (construct size and shape; beat rate for cardiac tissue).
Mid time point: chamber B fixed and cooled as for chamber A. Optional test compound added to chamber C; chamber D stays as the untreated control.
Days 8-12: continue feeding, sensing and imaging; robotic-arm moves scheduled outside imaging windows.
End point: chamber C fixed in paraformaldehyde and later flushed with buffer; chamber D filled with RNA stabilizer. Whole bay then set to 4 C.
Lab operations end; bay held at 4 C through deorbit, splashdown and courier hand-over.

sample_return.note: Fixed and RNA-stabilized constructs and medium aliquots should stay at 4 C from the end of operations to the customer lab. About 20 min to the courier plus 1-2 days of transport fits within 72 h. Mechanical testing needs live, unfixed constructs. A live-return option would need the bay held near 37 C (or at a validated holding temperature) through recovery, which has not yet been demonstrated for LELP-1.

experiments.ground_control: An identical perfusion module in a ground bay with constructs from the same batch, run at 1 g on the same feeding, imaging and fixation timeline. It is offset by a few hours so it can replay the flight temperature log. Launch vibration and re-entry loads are replayed on a shaker where possible. An optional third group in a rotating-wall or clinostat setup separates flow and shear effects from gravity effects.

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source claim. Scaled down from flight perfusion systems: the Mir BTS (125 ml rotating perfused vessel, membrane gas exchanger, pH/pO2 monitoring) and the NASA Bioculture System (hollow-fiber perfusion cassettes with per-cassette temperature and flow control). Peak power: pumps 3 W, valves 2 W pulsed, camera and LED 5 W, sensors 1.5 W, electronics 2.5 W, cold pads about 8 W (to be confirmed by thermal analysis) = 22 W, within the 30 W large-bay limit. The 37 C hold uses the bay's own thermoelectric block. Mass 5.55 kg, within the 6.0 kg limit.

needs: Bay powered at 37 C during the pad wait and ascent, with late load no more than about 48 h before launch (live tissues)
Small 4 C cold pads and an insulated pocket inside the 37 C bay for fixed chambers and medium aliquots, since a bay holds only one setpoint
Image and sensor downlink on each ground pass so the ground team can adjust flow and feeding
Robotic-arm moves scheduled outside imaging and fixation windows to keep the bay near 1e-6 g
Optional: a small pre-charged 5% CO2 gas cartridge if a customer needs bicarbonate-buffered medium (not a standard bay service)
limitations: 14 days is short for tissue growth. The Mir cartilage ran 4 months after 3 months on Earth. LELP-1 suits early responses and method tests, not growing mature tissue.

Microgravity has not been shown to make better tissue. Mir cartilage was smaller and mechanically weaker, and ISS heart tissues lost contractile force. Customers should expect to study gravity effects, not to receive a better product.

No crew. On CRS-20 the crew exchanged medium by syringe; on LELP-1 every medium change and fixation must be automatic, and nobody can clear a blocked line. Gas bubbles do not rise in microgravity, so the flow path needs a bubble trap and fully automatic recovery.
No CO2 supply. The Mir BTS used 10% CO2 and the CRS-20 incubator used 5% CO2. HEPES-buffered medium changes metabolism compared with those setups, so the ground control must use the same medium.
Oxygen comes only from the sealed bay air, and the cells' CO2 builds up there. The gas budget must be sized for each customer, because cardiac tissue uses far more oxygen than cartilage.

Live tissue must wait about 2 days at the pad and survive ascent loads. Returned tissue is fixed or stabilized, so mechanical properties cannot be tested after return unless a live-return mode is developed.
Robotic-arm moves raise acceleration to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g.
Volumes are millilitres and there are 8 constructs per bay: a research-scale study, not production biomanufacturing.
In-line glucose/lactate sensing and the per-chamber cold pads are our design choices and have not flown on LELP-1.

corrections_to_leads: Freed et al. PNAS 1997 is confirmed. The paper calls the Mir hardware the 'Biotechnology System (BTS)', a rotating perfused bioreactor. It does not use the name 'Bioreactor Demonstration System', so we used the paper's name.

The Mir result was negative for tissue quality: Mir constructs were smaller and mechanically inferior. The entry does not claim microgravity grows better tissue.

NASA Bioculture System confirmed: hollow-fiber perfusion cassettes, validated on SpaceX-13 in December 2017, then CS-02 (SpaceX-18, 2019) and CS-04 (SpaceX-22, 2021). The pages we opened give no temperature range, no pH/oxygen/glucose sensor details and no in-flight fixation feature, so we do not claim them.

Commercial ISS bioreactors: we could not confirm flight details for any specific commercial bioreactor product. Sharma et al. names commercial partners (Space Tango, BioServe) but no bioreactor model, so none is listed as heritage.
The pH, dissolved-oxygen and glucose sensing in this entry is our design. The Mir BTS monitored pH and pO2; in-flight glucose sensing is not backed by the sources we opened.
On CRS-20, medium exchange and preservation were done by crew with syringes, not automatically.

Heart-tissue sample count: we did not open the press page that gives a count, so we use the paper's own numbers (20 flight and 16 ground tissues at the start). The paper reports that the beat irregularity went away after return, while the loss of force persisted.

experiments.title: Microfluidic lab-on-a-chip and organ-chips
experiments.why: Organ-chips are small devices where living human cells line tiny perfused channels, so they behave more like real tissue than a flat dish. NIH funds them so scientists can assess biomarkers, efficacy and toxicity of drugs before clinical trials. In orbit, astronauts show signs of accelerated ageing, and human tissue on chips has shown related changes, for example weaker, arrhythmic engineered heart tissue after a month on the ISS. Microgravity can therefore act as a stressor that brings out tissue damage and drug effects. Chips need only microlitres of fluid and simple pumps, which suits an automated, uncrewed lab.

Organ-chip and microphysiological-system makers that want flight data
Academic groups funded under programmes like NIH NCATS and ISS National Lab Tissue Chips in Space

heritage.mission: GeneSat-1 (NASA Ames)
heritage.what_flew: Microbes, to study gene expression in spaceflight
heritage.finding: An early NASA Ames biological cubesat. A 2019 NASA review groups it with PharmaSat, EcAMSat and BioSentinel as heritage for autonomous biology on small free-flyers.

heritage.mission: PharmaSat (NASA Ames)
heritage.what_flew: Yeast (S. cerevisiae) in 48 microfluidic wells dosed with several concentrations of the antifungal voriconazole, read by a 3-colour optical absorbance system at each well, inside a sealed 1.2 L payload vessel
heritage.finding: The team got in-orbit yeast growth curves at several drug doses and ran matched ground controls. This is the closest heritage for automated drug dosing and optical readout in microfluidic wells on a free-flyer.

heritage.mission: EcAMSat (NASA Ames / Stanford)
heritage.what_flew: Uropathogenic E. coli (wild type and a strain lacking the rpoS gene) grown in a fluidic card and then exposed to three doses of gentamicin
heritage.finding: Microgravity did not change growth rates. Both strains had slower metabolism in flight and were more susceptible to gentamicin, not more resistant. The rpoS-lacking strain was 34-37% less metabolically active than wild type on the ground and in flight. A ground test showed that multi-week storage in the payload hardware stressed the cells.

heritage.mission: BioSentinel (NASA Ames), on Artemis I
heritage.what_flew: Yeast housed in microfluidic cards, plus a radiation detector, to study the response to deep-space radiation
heritage.finding: Four two-week experiments ran, but no yeast grew. NASA traced this to the yeast expiring during long storage before launch, not to radiation. The lesson is that biology must be loaded late and launch slips must be limited.

heritage.platform: ISS (BioServe perfusion platform, sealed, three Nortis Triplex chips per unit)
heritage.what_flew: Human kidney proximal tubule cells from four donors in perfused 3-D chips. After 6 days of acclimation in orbit they got 2 days of 2% human serum, vitamin D, or plain medium. The chips were then fixed in orbit with RNAlater or formalin, and vitamin D effluent was frozen below -80 C on the ISS.
heritage.finding: Microgravity did not change how the cells processed vitamin D, and it caused no unique response to serum. The authors say these pathways are not significantly altered by short-term exposure and call for study of longer exposure. Mold contamination made about a third of the flight samples unusable.

heritage.mission: Tissue Chips in Space, engineered heart tissue (Johns Hopkins / Univ. of Washington), SpaceX CRS-20
heritage.platform: ISS (automated heart-on-a-chip chambers in sealed habitats inside an ISS incubator at 37 C and 5% CO2)
heritage.what_flew: Engineered heart tissues made from human iPSC-derived heart muscle cells, handed over live 2 days before launch and kept in orbit for about 30 days. Contraction was read in real time by magnets in flexible posts and magnetic sensors. Some tissues were fixed in orbit (PFA, stored at 4 C) or put in RNAlater (stored at -80 C).
heritage.finding: Flight tissues had significantly weaker twitch forces and more arrhythmias, plus sarcomere disruption and mitochondrial damage. Genes linked to heart failure, metabolic disorders, oxidative stress and inflammation went up. Beat irregularity returned to normal after return to Earth; sarcomere changes did not.

protocol.sample: Four to six human organ-chips supplied by the customer. Reference case: a kidney proximal tubule chip made with primary human tubule cells, with treated and vehicle chips side by side. The same layout works for liver, gut or heart chips.
protocol.container: Optically clear organ-chips on a fluidic manifold inside the BSL-2 triple-contained large bay, with a micro-pump per chip, bubble traps, valved reservoirs (medium, drug, fixative, RNA-stabilising reagent) and a cooled effluent-collection carousel
protocol.launch_state: Live, mature tissue under continuous perfusion at 37 C (finished organ-chips are not launched frozen; the ISS heart tissues were handed over live 2 days before launch). The bay is loaded late and stays powered through launch.
protocol.light_gas: No light needed except brief imaging LEDs. HEPES-buffered medium with no CO2 (the ISS heart study used 5% CO2, which LELP-1 cannot supply). Oxygen comes from gas-permeable chip walls and tubing exposed to the sealed bay air.

steps.action: Ground: customer seeds the chips and perfuses them until the tissue forms. Chips that fail barrier or imaging checks are rejected. Sterile assembly and leak checks, because nobody can remove a contaminated chip in orbit.
Late load: chips, filled reservoirs and the empty effluent carousel go into the large bay. The bay is sealed, held at 37 C and kept on power. The ground-control set is loaded the same way.
Launch. Pumps keep a low continuous flow and the bay holds 37 C through ascent. The robotic arm stays parked.
First in-orbit health check: brightfield image of every chip, check of flow and pressure for bubbles or blockage, first effluent fraction collected at 4 C.
Days 2-6: acclimation under perfusion (the ISS kidney study used 6 days). One brightfield and fluorescence image set per day. One effluent fraction per chip every 24 h into the 4 C carousel.
Dosing: the valves switch half the chips to medium containing the drug and half to vehicle medium. Imaging every 6 h.
Effluent fractions every 12 h for injury and inflammation markers. Image sets continue.
End point after 2 days of dosing: half the chips are flushed with an RNAlater-type RNA-stabilising reagent and half are fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. Lines are sealed and the bay drops to 4 C.
Bay held at 4 C through deorbit, re-entry and splashdown. Cassette goes to the customer's courier about 20 min after splashdown.

sample_return.note: Our estimate, not a source value. All chips are fixed or RNA-stabilised in orbit and effluent is collected at 4 C, so nothing needs to stay alive through return. The chain is held at 4 C: about 1 day in orbit after fixation, re-entry, about 20 min to the recovery ship, then 1-2 days to the lab. The ISS heart study stored PFA-fixed samples at 4 C, which matches this plan. But both ISS studies kept RNAlater samples or vitamin D effluent at -80 C, which LELP-1 cannot do. Customers must test RNA quality and labile markers after a 4 C hold of the same length on the ground, and the ground control must use the same hold times.

experiments.ground_control: Chips from the same cell lot and seeding batch run in an identical flight-spare bay on the ground, with the same pumps, reservoirs, flow rates, imaging schedule, dosing time and fixation time. The ground run follows the flight about 2 h behind, driven by the flight telemetry, and replays the recorded flight temperatures and 4 C hold durations. Where possible it also gets a launch-vibration profile and the same pre-launch storage time, so microgravity is the main difference. Extra chips stay in a standard CO2 incubator as a baseline for the hardware itself.

A cold chain at 4 C from bay to courier, with hold times logged so the ground control can match them
limitations: Short exposure: LELP-1 runs at most 14 days. The ISS heart study ran about 30 days. The ISS kidney study found no unique response after 6 days plus 2 days of treatment, and the authors call for study of longer exposure. Slow effects may not show up in a LELP-1 flight.
No crew: nobody can clear a bubble, re-prime a line or swap a leaking or contaminated chip. A failed chip is lost, so each condition needs at least two chips.

Live launch: mature organ-chips are launched live, so they must survive late loading, any launch slip and ascent at 37 C. BioSentinel lost its yeast to long pre-launch storage, and EcAMSat cells were stressed by multi-week storage, so launch-slip limits must be agreed with the customer.
No -80 C freezing in orbit: samples are fixed or RNA-stabilised and returned at 4 C. Both ISS chip studies froze some samples at -80 C. Markers that need frozen samples may degrade.

No CO2 or incubator gas control: the ISS heart tissues were kept at 5% CO2, but LELP-1 media must be HEPES-buffered and oxygen depends on gas-permeable chip materials. The customer must qualify the chip and medium in a sealed, CO2-free bay on the ground first. Some chip plastics (e.g. PDMS) may absorb small hydrophobic drugs, so the drug must also be qualified on the same chips.
No in-flight 1 g control: LELP-1 has no centrifuge, so the 1 g comparison is only on the ground, and launch, re-entry and radiation effects are mixed in with the microgravity effect.
Few chips per bay (about 4-6) and microlitre effluent volumes limit how many doses and assays one bay supports. Big dose-response studies need several bays.
Microgravity at the bay is good (about 1e-6 g) but drops to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g while the arm moves, so arm moves must be scheduled away from key steps.
The protocol and module here are a reference design in a digital twin. LELP-1 has not flown yet, and none of the heritage results above were obtained on LELP-1.

corrections_to_leads: Tissue Chips in Space did not start in 2018. NCATS and CASIS (now the ISS National Lab) set it up in October 2016, and the first chips launched in December 2018.

Kidney chip second flight: NCATS and the UW authors' blog agree it launched on CRS-22 on June 3, 2021 (the earlier lead said the blog gave 2022; it does not). Only first-flight (CRS-17, May 2019) results are cited.

Kidney chip method: the chips were fixed in orbit with RNAlater or formalin after 6 days of acclimation and 2 days of treatment; only the vitamin D effluent was frozen below -80 C on the ISS. The hardware was the BioServe perfusion platform. Mold contamination made about a third of flight samples unusable.

Kidney chip result: the published flight data found no unique microgravity response to serum and no change in vitamin D metabolism. It should not be described as showing kidney damage or kidney-stone changes in space.

Heart chip: tissues flew live on SpaceX CRS-20 (launch March 2020), were kept at 37 C and 5% CO2 in an ISS incubator for about 30 days, and contraction was read by magnet-in-post sensors. Beat irregularity recovered after return; sarcomere changes did not.

Lung, bone-marrow, blood-brain-barrier and gut chips: NCATS confirms these organ areas flew (May 2019 and March 2020 launches), but their published results were not checked. They appear only as programme scope, not as findings.

BioSentinel (2022, Artemis I) produced no biology result. The yeast did not grow, which NASA traced to long pre-launch storage. The NASA page does not say the yeast was dried and rehydrated, so that detail was dropped.

EcAMSat (2017) found E. coli MORE susceptible to gentamicin in flight, not more resistant. Growth rates were unchanged. The 34-37% lower activity of the rpoS mutant is relative to wild type in all conditions, not a flight effect.
PharmaSat: launch year 2009 is confirmed; the Minotaur I launch vehicle was not confirmed on an opened agency or paper page and was removed.
GeneSat-1: the opened source only says it launched in 2006 to study gene expression in microbes; details of its culture and optical system were removed.

GeneSat-1 (2006), PharmaSat (2009) and EcAMSat (2017) flew microfluidic wells and cards with microbes, not human organ-chips. They are heritage for automation, dosing and optical readout only.

experiments.title: Cell mechanobiology: how cells sense gravity and load
experiments.why: Cells sense load through the actin cytoskeleton, focal adhesions and the nucleus. When that load changes, their gene expression and behaviour change too. On Earth this matters for bone loss, blood vessel disease and ageing. In space, bone and blood vessel cells lose their normal load. Flight studies show actin changes within seconds of microgravity, and changes in adhesion, stress and metabolism genes after days. Only free fall removes the gravity load for days. Ground devices such as clinostats only turn the gravity vector, and in one osteocyte study they did not reproduce the flight changes. An on-board 1 g centrifuge gives a control that shares launch, radiation and hardware, so the effect of gravity can be separated from the other spaceflight factors.

Space agency life-science programmes studying astronaut bone loss and cardiovascular deconditioning

Ground runs in the NASA rotating-wall-vessel did not adequately reproduce the flight changes.

protocol.sample: Adherent human endothelial cells (primary HUVEC or an immortalised endothelial line) carrying two live reporters: Lifeact-GFP for F-actin and H2B-mCherry for the nucleus. Option: swap in an osteocyte line (for example Ocy454) for a bone customer. One frozen cell lot feeds the flight 0 g bay, the flight 1 g centrifuge bay and the ground bays.
protocol.container: 0 g bay: 24-well glass-bottom cassette, fibronectin-coated, with gas-permeable lids, in the sealed BSL-2 bay. 1 g bay: a 24-well ring cassette on the centrifuge rotor, all wells at one 8 cm radius with well floors facing outward. Each bay has its own -80 C passive cryo cassette with cells until thaw. Reservoirs: HEPES-buffered growth medium, wash buffer, 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA), PBS, RNAlater-type stabiliser, waste.
protocol.launch_state: Cryopreserved cells (-80 C passive cassette); media and fixatives at 4 C bay setpoint
protocol.light_gas: No growth light needed. The bay stays dark except for short microscope LED exposures, kept low to limit phototoxicity. No CO2: 25 mM HEPES-buffered medium with gas-permeable lids and the sealed bay air headspace.

steps.action: Launch with cells frozen at -80 C and fluids at 4 C. In orbit: bay checkout, seal and pressure check, dosimeter on. Spin up the 1 g centrifuge bay and confirm 1.0 g at the ring radius from rotor speed and its accelerometer.

Set both bays to 37 C. Thaw cells automatically, dilute out the cryoprotectant, seed into the fibronectin-coated wells. In the 1 g bay, cells are delivered through the rotary fluid coupling and attach on the spinning rotor. In the 0 g bay: brightfield + GFP + mCherry images every 1 h for 12 h, then every 3 h.
Replace medium to remove cryoprotectant and unattached cells. Keep time-lapse imaging. Hold robotic arm moves outside imaging windows and log every arm move against well images.
Early end point: fix 8 wells per bay with 4% PFA for 15 min, then flush to PBS. The 1 g wells are fixed while still spinning.
Medium change. Continue time-lapse imaging of the live wells: cell area, shape, actin stress fibres, nuclear area and shape.

Last live images. Move conditioned medium to a reservoir. Fix 8 wells per bay with PFA then PBS; stabilise 8 wells per bay with RNAlater-type reagent. Fix and stabilise the 1 g wells before stopping the rotor. Then set both bays to 4 C.

Robotic arm takes the fixed 0 g bay to the central 40x fluorescence microscope for higher-resolution images of actin and nuclear shape, then returns it. Repeat for the stopped, fixed 1 g bay. Hold at 4 C until de-orbit.
De-orbit, splashdown, bays removed. Samples handed to the customer courier about 20 min after splashdown and carried at 4 C to the lab (about 1-2 days).

sample_return.note: Our planning values, not a source claim. PFA-fixed wells held in PBS at 4 C are the robust part and can wait up to about 2 weeks. The RNA-stabilised wells are the limit: aim to reach the lab within about 7 days of stabilisation on day 7. With de-orbit on day 9 and 1-2 days of courier time, that is about 3-4 days. The 4 C hold of the chosen stabiliser must be validated in the ground runs. Do not freeze the fixed glass-bottom cassettes. Keep the conditioned medium at 4 C and assay it soon after arrival.

experiments.ground_control: Two controls run together. (1) In-flight 1 g control: a second large bay with a small centrifuge holds the same cells at 1.0 g for the whole run. This control shares launch, radiation, the sealed bay and the timeline, so the 0 g vs 1 g difference is the effect of gravity (the approach used in the KUBIK T-cell study, where 1 g samples sat in the central centrifuge positions). (2) Ground control: flight-like 0 g and centrifuge bays in a lab at 37 C, with the same cell lot, media and fluidics script. They replay the flight timeline from telemetry a few hours behind, including real temperature changes and any missed steps. Clinostat or random positioning runs can be added, but they do not replace flight: in the osteocyte study, rotating-wall-vessel runs did not adequately reproduce the flight changes.

items.item: LumaScope-class inverted microscope (brightfield + 2 fluorescence channels) with XY stage and camera
24-well fibronectin-coated glass-bottom cassette with gas-permeable lids
-80 C passive cryo cassette with cells
Filled fluid reservoirs (medium, wash, 4% PFA, PBS, RNA stabiliser, waste)
Pumps, valves and manifold

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source figure. This is the 0 g bay. The microscope is about 40% of the mass (our estimate for a compact LumaScope-class unit). Fluid volumes cover two medium changes, fixation and stabilisation of 24 wells. Peak power is about 10 W for LED and camera, 6 W for pumps, 4 W for the stage and 2-4 W for the controller. Imaging and pumping are scheduled apart so the load stays under the 30 W large-bay limit. We assume the bay's 25 W thermoelectric block, which holds 37 C, is a bay service outside the 30 W payload budget; this must be confirmed. The 1 g control needs a second large bay (see needs).

needs: An on-board 1 g reference centrifuge: this is not a standard bay service. Smallest option (our estimate): a second large bay with a balanced mini-centrifuge, 8 cm radius at about 106 rpm for 1.0 g, carrying a 24-well ring cassette with all wells at the same radius and well floors facing outward. About 5.3 kg (motor and rotor 1.5 kg, ring cassette 0.8 kg, -80 C cryo cassette with cells 0.6 kg, fluidics with reservoirs and rotary coupling 1.2 kg, controller 0.3 kg, structure and containment 0.9 kg) and about 14 W peak. That fits the 6.0 kg / 30 W large-bay limit.

Do not lay plate-format 12-well cassettes flat on an 8 cm rotor: their wells would sit at roughly 5.4 to 10.6 cm radius, about 0.7 to 1.3 g across the cassette (our calculation). The ring layout keeps g on the cell layer within about 1%.
Fixation and stabilisation must work on the spinning rotor (rotating fluid coupling or reservoirs on the rotor), so the 1 g samples are never stopped before preservation

Vibration isolation and dynamic balancing of the centrifuge bay, placement far from the 0 g bay, and accelerometer logging to show the 0 g bay stays near 1e-6 g. Attitude control must absorb the rotor's spin-up momentum (small, about 0.07 N m s for a 1 kg rotor at 8 cm, our estimate), or the rotor needs a counter-rotating mass.
The 40x central-lab microscope must accept the 1 g ring cassette after fixation, so both arms get the same high-resolution images
Arm-move blackout windows during live-imaging and fixation steps, with every arm move time-stamped in the science data
Optional: the same centrifuge run at 0.16 g (about 42 rpm) or 0.38 g (about 65 rpm) for a partial-gravity series (Moon, Mars)
Optional: live imaging on the centrifuge (a small camera on the rotor, or short stops under 2 minutes) if the customer wants a 1 g time-lapse and not only end points
limitations: Cells launch frozen and attach in orbit, so the experiment cannot catch the seconds-scale actin response at the onset of microgravity seen on TEXUS rockets. A 1 g to 0 g step on the rotor could, but only with live imaging on the centrifuge.
Attaching and spreading after an in-orbit thaw is itself a variable. The 1 g centrifuge bay controls for it, but results describe cells that attached in microgravity, not cells adapted from 1 g.
A small-radius centrifuge is not a perfect 1 g: g changes with radius through the medium height, and there are Coriolis forces and spin-up/stop transients. These must be reported with the data.

Robotic arm moves give 1e-4 to 1e-3 g. That is equal to or worse than the 1e-4 to 1e-5 g reported on TEXUS-54 and 100-1000 times above the quiet bay level, so arm moves must stay out of key windows and be logged.
2 to 14 days covers early and mid-term responses only. Slower processes such as osteocyte maturation in a mineralised 3D matrix over weeks or months need longer missions.
The passive -80 C cassettes must hold temperature from late loading until thaw on day 1. Their 0.6 kg mass is our estimate and must be checked against the real hold time.
No crew: there is no manual rescue of a blocked line, bubble or contaminated well. The design relies on extra wells and automated checks.

The bay microscope (brightfield + 2 fluorescence channels) cannot resolve single focal adhesions live. Adhesion and YAP/TAZ readouts are post-flight end points on fixed cells, and 40x central-lab images are taken only after fixation.
No CO2 supply: cells must tolerate HEPES-buffered medium in a sealed bay, which can shift pH and metabolism compared with a standard incubator. The ground control must use the same medium.

Only fixed and stabilised samples come back in good shape. Live cells for functional tests after flight are not part of this protocol, because the return takes days and re-entry and splashdown loads would add artefacts.

experiments.title: Biofilm formation on spacecraft and medical materials
experiments.why: Bacteria that settle on a surface build a slime-covered community called a biofilm. On Earth these films clog pipes and filters and cause device-related infections, and they are much harder to kill than free-floating cells. In spacecraft the same films can grow in water lines and life-support hardware; NASA states that biofilm formation can cause equipment malfunction and human illnesses. Microgravity removes sedimentation and buoyancy-driven flow, which changes how cells and oxygen reach a surface. Two flight experiments with the same strain, run with different growth media, reported opposite results, so the question is still open. A free-flyer lets a materials or device maker fly coupons of their own surface, run an identical module on the ground, and get the fixed coupons back for imaging.

Medical device makers testing catheter-grade silicone and other indwelling-device surfaces

heritage.mission: STS-132 and STS-135 (Space Shuttle Atlantis)
heritage.what_flew: Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 in BioServe Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) units inside Group Activation Packs, housed in a Commercial Generic Bioprocessing Apparatus. Biofilms grew on a 13 mm mixed cellulose ester membrane in modified artificial urine medium with 6 mM sodium nitrate as terminal electron acceptor, static, 37 C for 72 h, then cooled to 8 C and fixed with 9% paraformaldehyde. Some units used solid inserts (no gas exchange), others gas-exchange inserts.
heritage.finding: Spaceflight increased viable cells about three-fold (p<0.01) and increased biofilm biomass and thickness. Flight biofilms showed a structure of columns overlaid with a canopy, not reported before in static culture on Earth. A flagella-motility mutant did not form that structure. With gas-exchange inserts (more oxygen) no flight-versus-ground difference was seen.

heritage.mission: Space Biofilms (bacterial part), ISS
heritage.year: Launched November 2019 on Cygnus NG-12, returned early 2020 on SpaceX CRS-19; papers 2022 and 2023
heritage.what_flew: P. aeruginosa PA14 in FPAs inside Group Activation Packs, incubated in BioServe's Space Automated Bioproduct Lab. Six materials: stainless steel 316, passivated SS316, a lubricant-impregnated surface, catheter-grade silicone with and without a laser-patterned microtopography, and cellulose membrane. Inoculum held in stasis in PBS (OD595 0.001) at 4 C, activated on orbit by the crew, grown 1, 2 or 3 days at 37 C in LB Lennox with 0.86% potassium nitrate in sealed chambers that force anaerobic growth, then terminated on orbit with 4% paraformaldehyde (morphology) or RNAlater (transcriptomics). Fixed samples were kept at 4 C; preserved samples at -80 C on orbit and returned at -20 C.
heritage.finding: On stainless steel and on the lubricant-impregnated surface, flight biofilms had significantly lower biomass and thickness than 1 g controls (p<=0.05), the opposite direction to the 2013 shuttle result, under a different medium. The lubricant-impregnated surface strongly reduced biofilm compared with stainless steel, more so in flight than on the ground; the authors propose it prevents the first stage, cell attachment. Passivated and plain SS316 showed no morphological difference.

heritage.mission: Space Biofilms (bacterial part), ISS - silicone and cellulose samples
heritage.what_flew: Catheter-grade silicone (1 cm2), silicone with a 3 um line-like laser interference pattern (0.635 cm2) and cellulose membrane (1.4 cm discs), grown 1, 2 and 3 days at 37 C, fixed with paraformaldehyde on orbit and imaged after return.
heritage.finding: Microgravity did not change the overall 3-D form of the biofilms; form depended on the material and its topography. The column-and-canopy structure was not observed, and the 3 um line pattern did not reduce biofilm on silicone. The authors leave open whether a more robust biofilm would have shown the canopy structure.

protocol.sample: Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 (BSL-2 model biofilm organism) plus a customer coupon panel: up to 24 coupons of about 1 cm2, for example stainless steel 316, catheter-grade silicone, a candidate coating and a cellulose membrane reference
protocol.container: 24-well sealed cassette in one large bay. Each well has a glass window on the bottom and holds one coupon above it; three fluid lines serve each well: growth medium, 4% paraformaldehyde, and RNA preservative, plus a shared PBS line for post-fixation washing and staining
protocol.launch_state: Live inoculum held in stasis in PBS at 4 C (not frozen), diluted to about OD595 0.001; medium, fixative and preservative loaded cold in separate sealed reservoirs; coupons cleaned, sterilised by a method each material tolerates, and mounted in the cassette
protocol.light_gas: No light needed; wells kept dark except during microscope imaging. No CO2 and no gas supply: the cassette is sealed and the medium carries nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor, so growth becomes anaerobic, as in both heritage flights. An aerobic variant with gas-permeable well lids is flown as a separate bay; on the shuttle, more oxygen removed the flight-ground difference.

steps.action: After orbit insertion and attitude settling, the bay ramps from 4 C to 37 C over about 2 h. Pumps fill all 24 wells with medium over the coupons, then inject the stasis inoculum. Static growth starts; first brightfield images and a transmission turbidity reading are taken.
Daily automated run: brightfield image stack of each well through the glass window, turbidity reading, and a log of bay temperature, pressure, seal state, dosimeter dose and accelerometer data.
Repeat the daily imaging and sensor run. No pumping or arm motion is scheduled, to keep the quasi-steady level near 1e-6 g.

Repeat the daily run. Optional single transfer of the bay by the robotic arm to the central 40x microscope for a closer look at two wells; the arm motion is logged because it raises acceleration to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g.
Repeat the daily run.

Termination. Twelve wells receive 4% paraformaldehyde and twelve receive RNA preservative, added directly as in the ISS heritage, with no rinse first. After about 1 h the fixed wells are washed with PBS, stained with a nucleic-acid dye and a lipid dye, and imaged on both bay fluorescence channels. The bay then cools to 4 C and holds there.
Hold at 4 C. Housekeeping data only; seal and pressure checks confirm containment before deorbit.
Deorbit, entry, splashdown and recovery. The sealed cassette stays at 4 C until handover to the customer courier on the recovery ship.

in_flight.name: Biofilm growth over time
in_flight.method: Daily brightfield image stacks on the bay inverted microscope through each glass window. This shows the film on the window (a reference surface) and on transparent coupons; films on opaque coupons are measured after return

in_flight.name: Structure at termination
in_flight.method: Two-channel fluorescence imaging after on-orbit staining of the fixed wells (nucleic-acid dye and lipid dye), optionally repeated at 40x in the central lab microscope

in_flight.name: Free-floating cell density
in_flight.method: Transmission turbidity reading per well, as a rough proxy for planktonic growth

in_flight.name: Culture environment
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure, humidity and seal sensors logged continuously; confirms the 37 C hold and containment

in_flight.name: Mechanical and radiation environment
in_flight.method: Three-axis accelerometer (quasi-steady level and arm-motion events) and active silicon dosimeter plus passive TLDs in the bay

in_flight.name: Termination timing
in_flight.method: Valve and pump telemetry records when fixative or preservative reached each well; the ground control is matched to this

post_flight.name: Biomass, mean thickness and surface coverage
post_flight.method: Confocal laser scanning microscopy of the fixed coupons stained for nucleic acids and lipids, quantified with COMSTAT-type image analysis, as in the heritage work

post_flight.name: Surface topography of film and coupon
post_flight.method: Scanning electron microscopy on fixed coupons; also shows whether the coating or texture survived the run

post_flight.name: Gene expression
post_flight.method: RNA extraction and RNA-seq from the preservative-filled wells, compared with the ground control

post_flight.name: Attachment pattern on textured or coated surfaces
post_flight.method: High-resolution confocal microscopy of the patterned and coated coupons to see whether cells attached in or between features

post_flight.name: Material damage
post_flight.method: Surface inspection after cleaning and, if the customer asks, profilometry of coupons before and after flight

post_flight.name: Viable count (optional)
post_flight.method: Plate counts from one unfixed well. The count reflects survival through two days at 4 C, not the state at day 5

sample_return.note: Fixed and preserved wells come back in the sealed cassette at 4 C, the lowest the bay can hold. Fixation is on day 5 and splashdown on day 7; the cassette reaches the courier about 20 min after splashdown and the lab 1-2 days later, so about 4-5 days pass from preservation to the lab. Fixed samples tolerate this; on ISS the fixed samples were held at 4 C for weeks before return. The ISS RNA samples were kept at -80 C on orbit and returned at -20 C; LELP-1 bays cannot freeze, so RNA stays in preservative at 4 C and quality may be lower unless a passive -80 C return cassette is flown.

experiments.ground_control: An identical flight-spare module runs at the Swiss ground segment with the same cassette, coupons, medium lot and inoculum, started about 2 h after the flight module and terminated on the same offset. The recorded flight temperature profile is played back on the ground unit. A third, non-inoculated cassette is put through the launch vibration and entry load profile to show coupons and seals survive. The bay has no on-orbit centrifuge, so the ground 1 g run is the only gravity reference; the two heritage flights disagreeing shows why that matters.

Pump and valve manifold with per-well addressing
LumaScope-class inverted microscope head, LED illumination and two-axis stage
Thermal interface plate and insulation for the 37 C hold
Triple-containment housing, seals and absorbent layer (BSL-2)
Avionics, harness, sensors and dosimeter

module.basis: OUR ESTIMATE for LELP-1, not a source number. Items add to 6.00 kg, the large-bay limit. Peak 28 W is the worst case during the day-0 ramp to 37 C: 20 W thermoelectric, 4 W pumps and valves, 3 W microscope and LED, 1 W avionics; under the 30 W large-bay limit. Steady draw while holding 37 C is lower and imaging is duty-cycled once a day. Fluid volumes follow the heritage FPA loads (2.75 mL medium and 1.75 mL termination fluid per sample) scaled to 24 wells with margin. Three fixation time points, as on ISS, need three such modules, which fits in the 16 large bays.

needs: Glass-window wells and coupon carriers; in-flight imaging sees the window and transparent coupons, opaque coupons are read after return
Two termination lines per well, so morphology (paraformaldehyde) and transcriptomics (RNA preservative) come from the same run
A PBS line and waste volume for washing fixed wells before on-orbit staining
Sealed, gas-tight wells for the anaerobic case, plus a gas-permeable lid option for an aerobic bay; no gas bottle needed
On-orbit stain injection (nucleic-acid and lipid dyes) for the fluorescence channels
Stowage at 4 C from loading to orbit, not -80 C, since the inoculum launches live
A passive -80 C or -20 C return cassette if the customer wants frozen RNA, because the bay stops at 4 C
Two or three identical modules for more than one fixation time point
Accelerometer logging tied to robotic-arm activity
limitations: Two to fourteen days is short for this field. Spacecraft water-system biofilms build up over months, so the flight shows early attachment and growth, not mature fouling or long-term material damage.
No crew. Everything runs on a timer, so there is no re-dosing if a well looks wrong and no fixing a stuck valve.
One fixation point per well set. A time course needs several bays or relies on the daily in-flight images, which are lower resolution than post-flight confocal.
The bay cannot freeze. RNA stays in preservative at 4 C rather than frozen as on ISS, so transcriptomics may be weaker unless a passive cold cassette is flown.
No in-flight 1 g control. Without a centrifuge, the only reference is the ground run, and the heritage flights show flight-versus-ground results on this organism can go either way.
Static culture only. The bay has no flow loop, so it does not reproduce flowing water or condensate lines where spacecraft biofilms form.
In-flight imaging cannot see films on opaque coupons; those are measured only after return.
Entry and splashdown loads act on fixed films. Shear or sloshing can detach or smear them; the non-inoculated cassette on the ground load test is the only check.
24 wells per bay gives a few replicates per material: enough for clear effects, not for small ones or dose-response work.
Results may be material-specific. On ISS, biofilm form depended on the material, not on gravity.

The column-and-canopy structure is not a safe expectation. It was reported on the shuttle flights and not seen on ISS with the same strain and an anaerobic setup but a different medium, so we do not promise it.

corrections_to_leads: The Kim et al. lead is correct: PLoS ONE 8(4): e62437, 2013, P. aeruginosa PA14 on STS-132 and STS-135 (Space Shuttle Atlantis), 72 h static at 37 C, column-and-canopy structure, dependent on flagella-driven motility.

The NASA-funded Space Biofilms ISS run (launched November 2019 on Cygnus NG-12, returned early 2020 on SpaceX CRS-19) did not confirm the 2013 result. Flight biofilms on stainless steel and on the lubricant-impregnated surface had significantly lower biomass and thickness than 1 g controls, and the column-and-canopy structure was not observed. Enhanced biofilm growth in microgravity must not be presented as settled.

The ISS run used a different medium from the shuttle flights: LB Lennox with 0.86% potassium nitrate, not modified artificial urine medium with 6 mM sodium nitrate. Both were anaerobic sealed setups, but they were not matched in medium.

The fungal part of Space Biofilms (Penicillium rubens) used 24-well plates rather than FPAs. The CU Boulder page dates the fungal launch to February 2022 on NG-17; the NASA page lists NG-12 as the original flight and NG-17 as a partial re-flight.
In the 2013 shuttle work, gas-exchange inserts (more oxygen) removed the flight-ground difference entirely, so the oxygen condition is part of the claim.

Fixation at time points with post-flight confocal imaging matches the heritage (4% paraformaldehyde or RNAlater at 1, 2 and 3 days). ISS kept fixed samples at 4 C and preserved samples at -80 C on orbit, returning them at -20 C; LELP-1 bays cannot go below 4 C.

experiments.title: Microalgae and cyanobacteria for oxygen and food
experiments.why: Long crewed missions cannot carry all their oxygen and food from Earth. Photosynthetic microbes such as the cyanobacterium Limnospira indica (spirulina) and the green alga Chlorella take up carbon dioxide, release oxygen and make edible, protein-rich biomass. Engineers need flight data on growth rate, oxygen output, purity and gene or protein changes before they size a bioreactor for a habitat. In microgravity there is no buoyancy-driven mixing and gas bubbles do not rise, so a flight test shows whether a reactor design still delivers light, nutrients and gas transfer the way the models predict.
customers: Space-agency life support programmes that study bioregenerative systems, such as ESA's MELiSSA project
University and institute groups that study algal and cyanobacterial physiology in space (for example the ICGEB New Delhi groups that flew experiments on Axiom-4)
Companies building photobioreactors or algal food and feed products that want flight data on their hardware or strain
Groups testing nutrient recycling from waste streams, such as urea as a nitrogen source

heritage.mission: Arthrospira-B (ESA ArtEMISS project, MELiSSA)
heritage.what_flew: Limnospira indica PCC 8005 in four batch photobioreactors of about 50 ml each. Each reactor had a gas chamber and a liquid chamber separated by a PTFE membrane. Launched in December 2017 and run for about a month, with 16 batches in total.
heritage.finding: First experiment in space to measure both oxygen production rate and growth online. Oxygen production was tracked by the pressure rise in the gas chamber. The ground model fitted the flight data well early in each batch, but later in each batch oxygen output was lower than predicted. The authors linked this to bicarbonate running low and pH rising. They concluded that microgravity had no first-order effect on oxygen production rate. ESA reported that all returned samples were pure.

heritage.mission: PBR@LSR algae photobioreactor experiment (University of Stuttgart IRS, Airbus, DLR)
heritage.platform: ISS (linked to the Life Support Rack)
heritage.what_flew: A Chlorella vulgaris photobioreactor that took part of the CO2 removed by the Life Support Rack. It was designed to run for up to 180 days and launched in the second quarter of 2019.
heritage.finding: Operations began in June 2019, with a ground experiment running in parallel in Stuttgart. An unexpected loss of power supply ended the run after two weeks. Samples from those weeks came back on SpX-18 for analysis.

heritage.mission: Axiom Mission 4 (Ax-4), ICGEB New Delhi experiments under ISRO-NASA and ISRO-ESA arrangements
heritage.what_flew: Three edible microalgae (Chlorella sorokiniana-I, Parachlorella kessleri-I, Dysmorphococcus globosus-HI) under ISRO-NASA, and two cyanobacteria (Spirulina subsalsa, Synechococcus sp. PCC 11901) under ISRO-ESA, with the cyanobacteria grown on urea as the nitrogen source.
heritage.finding: ISRO reported that the microalgae and cyanobacteria experiments were completed as planned. We found no published results to cite yet.

protocol.sample: Limnospira indica PCC 8005 (axenic culture, the MELiSSA strain). A Chlorella strain can be flown instead in the same hardware.
protocol.container: Four flat-panel membrane photobioreactors (about 40 ml liquid each, 15 mm deep). Each has a liquid chamber and a gas headspace separated by a hydrophobic PTFE membrane. They sit in a large-bay cassette with an LED panel, a recirculation pump, and optical-density and oxygen sensors.
protocol.launch_state: Live culture at low density in bicarbonate-rich medium, kept dark at 10 C to slow growth until activation (our design choice; ground tests must confirm the culture survives the hold)
protocol.light_gas: Red/white LED light at about 35 to 80 umol photons m-2 s-1, set per reactor (our choice). Carbon comes from bicarbonate in the medium because the sealed bay has no CO2 supply. Oxygen collects in each reactor's headspace and is measured by pressure and an optical O2 sensor. Each headspace has a pressure relief; Arthrospira-B used 1.15 bar.

steps.action: Launch with reactors filled, lights off, bay held at 10 C. Log temperature, acceleration and dose.
After orbit checkout, warm to 33 C, start recirculation mixing and switch on the LEDs. Reactors 1-2 at 35 umol photons m-2 s-1, reactors 3-4 at 70 umol photons m-2 s-1.
Start logging optical density every 30 min, and headspace pressure and O2 every 5 min. Take a baseline microscope image of each reactor's sampling window.
Pump 2 ml from each reactor into fixative wells (for RNA/protein) and image trichome shape and chlorophyll autofluorescence.
Repeat sampling and imaging. If a headspace nears its pressure limit, vent it through the bay's relief path and log the vented volume.
Replace 20 ml of culture in reactors 3-4 with fresh medium from the reservoir (semi-continuous mode) to test growth after dilution and bicarbonate top-up.
Final sampling into fixative wells and final imaging.
Switch off the LEDs, stop mixing, cool the bay to 4 C. Live culture stays in the reactors for viability and purity tests on the ground.
Hold at 4 C through deorbit, splashdown and handover to the customer's courier.

in_flight.name: Growth (biomass)
in_flight.method: Optical density at about 750 nm, measured by LED and photodiode across each flat reactor and logged every 30 min

in_flight.name: Oxygen production rate
in_flight.method: Headspace pressure rise in each reactor (the Arthrospira-B approach), cross-checked with an optical O2 sensor spot

in_flight.name: Cell shape and pigment
in_flight.method: The bay's LumaScope-class microscope: brightfield for trichome length and coiling, and a fluorescence channel for chlorophyll and phycocyanin autofluorescence

in_flight.name: Culture conditions
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, light (LED current and a PAR photodiode), acceleration log and active dosimeter dose rate

post_flight.name: Dry weight and productivity
post_flight.method: Filter and dry the remaining culture; compare with the in-flight OD curve

post_flight.name: Pigments and protein
post_flight.method: Chlorophyll, carotenoid and phycocyanin by spectrophotometry; total protein content

post_flight.name: Purity
post_flight.method: Plating and 16S rRNA sequencing to detect contaminants

post_flight.name: pH and bicarbonate
post_flight.method: pH and dissolved inorganic carbon of the returned medium, to explain any late-batch slowdown

post_flight.name: Gene and protein expression
post_flight.method: Transcriptomics and proteomics on fixed samples from days 4, 7 and 10

post_flight.name: Viability
post_flight.method: Regrowth of the live returned culture under standard ground conditions

post_flight.name: Passive dose
post_flight.method: Read-out of the bay TLDs

sample_return.note: Fixed samples and live culture both stay at 4 C and in the dark. Cool-down is on day 11, splashdown about a day later, and the courier needs 1-2 days, so plan for up to about 96 h from cool-down to the lab. The live culture is only for viability and purity; fixed samples tolerate longer. This is our estimate and must be confirmed by the customer's ground tests.

experiments.ground_control: An identical flight-model module runs on the ground at the same time. It uses the same culture lot, medium batch, light settings, temperature profile (replayed from flight telemetry, including the 10 C launch hold and 4 C return) and sampling times. Optional: a second set of reactors on a 1 g centrifuge in flight would separate microgravity effects from launch and radiation effects.

limitations: The sealed bay has no CO2 supply, so growth is batch or semi-continuous on bicarbonate in the medium. It cannot copy a reactor fed by cabin CO2 the way PBR@LSR was. Arthrospira-B saw oxygen output drop late in each batch, which its authors linked to bicarbonate limitation.
12 days and about 160 ml of culture cannot test the months-long stability a real life support reactor needs. PBR@LSR was designed for up to 180 days.
No crew: bubbles, membrane fouling or a stuck pump cannot be fixed by hand. Running four reactors in parallel is the only backup.
No pH probe or pH control in this design (Arthrospira-B had none either), so pH drift is only measured after return.
There is too little biomass to test taste, food safety or feeding. Only composition and purity can be checked.
The live culture must survive a dark hold at launch and several days of cold return. This may bias viability and gene expression results.
Radiation in a 550 km sun-synchronous orbit differs from the ISS, so dose results do not compare directly with ISS data.
Robotic-arm moves raise acceleration to about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g. Arm activity should pause during key measurements.

experiments.title: Human heart muscle cells from stem cells
experiments.why: Some drugs were withdrawn from the market because they caused arrhythmias and sudden death. Drug developers now check cardiac safety on heart muscle cells made from human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC-CMs), as in the FDA-backed CiPA approach. Spaceflight is linked to a decline in cardiovascular function. On the ISS, flown hiPSC-CMs showed altered calcium handling and irregular beating. Engineered heart tissues also showed weaker contraction and mitochondrial damage, and the CRS-20 study said these changes mimic cardiac aging. Microgravity can stress human heart cells without drugs or genetic changes. This lets researchers study early disease-like changes and test whether compounds protect against them or behave differently.
customers: Pharma and CRO cardiac safety teams that already run hiPSC-CM assays (the FDA-backed CiPA approach checks its predictions in these cells)
Makers of hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and heart-on-a-chip systems who want to show how their models perform in space
Academic cardiology, cardiac aging and stem-cell labs
Space agencies and commercial crew programmes studying the cardiovascular risks of spaceflight

heritage.mission: SpaceX CRS-9 (Stanford, Joseph C. Wu lab)
heritage.what_flew: Beating 2D monolayers of hiPSC-CMs from 3 donors in sealed 6-well BioCells inside a Plate Habitat (PHAB). They were cultured in the SABL incubator at 37 C and 5% CO2 for 5.5 weeks, with the medium changed weekly. Video microscopy was done at 1.5 and 2.5 weeks on the ISS. Some cells were preserved in RNAlater in flight at 4.5 weeks, and others came back live.
heritage.finding: Beat rate was similar to ground controls in flight after 2.5 weeks, and contraction and relaxation velocities did not differ. Calcium handling changed: calcium transients decayed more slowly and beat intervals were more irregular, measured 3 days after live return. 2,635 genes were differentially expressed among flight, post-flight and ground samples, and mitochondrial pathways were enriched. Sarcomere structure did not differ significantly. After return to normal gravity, the gene-expression pattern reverted to one similar to ground controls, but mitochondrial pathways were still enriched.

heritage.mission: SpaceX CRS-20 (Tissue Chips in Space; Johns Hopkins and University of Washington, Deok-Ho Kim lab)
heritage.what_flew: 3D engineered heart tissues made from hiPSC-CMs (20 flight, 16 ground control at the start), each hung between two posts in an automated heart-on-a-chip. A magnet in one post and giant magnetoresistive sensors recorded contraction in real time without imaging. The tissues sat in PHABs inside SABL at 37 C and 5% CO2 for about 30 days. At 12, 19 and 26 days after launch the medium was changed and samples were preserved in 4% PFA or RNAlater. Two days after splashdown, live tissues were retrieved and hand-carried at 37 C and 5% CO2 to the University of Washington. They were kept for another 7 days at 1 g, to 9 days after return.
heritage.finding: Flight tissues had significantly lower twitch force and more arrhythmia (larger beat-interval changes) while on the ISS. They had shorter sarcomeres, and over 50% of their mitochondria had abnormal structure, against fewer than 10% in controls. Genes for inflammation, oxidative stress and heart failure went up, and genes for contractility and calcium signalling went down. The force deficit was still present 9 days after return, while the arrhythmia appeared to resolve.

protocol.sample: Commercial or customer hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, plated as beating 2D monolayers in a 24-well glass-bottom plate. Optionally, a line that carries a genetically encoded calcium reporter (customer's choice). A 3D engineered-heart-tissue chip is possible only if the customer supplies flight-qualified post-and-sensor hardware.
protocol.container: Sealed 24-well glass-bottom cassette (large bay) with gas-permeable lids, connected to the bay fluidics. Reservoirs hold HEPES-buffered maintenance medium, test compound and vehicle, 4% paraformaldehyde and RNA stabilizer, and there is a waste bag. The bay microscope views the cassette from below.
protocol.launch_state: Live, attached and beating at 37 C (late load). Thawing frozen cells in orbit is not recommended. One major supplier (Takara Cellartis) specifies storage at -150 C, the thaw includes a centrifuge step, and cells are ready for use only from day 3 after thawing.
protocol.light_gas: Dark except during imaging, when the microscope LED is on for seconds per well. There is no CO2 supply, so the cells use HEPES-buffered medium and gas-permeable lids, with the sealed bay's air headspace supplying oxygen. Medium changes every 2 days keep oxygen and nutrients up and remove lactate.

steps.action: Ground: thaw cells and plate them into the flight cassette. Plate the ground-control cassette from the same lot at the same time. Change medium every 2-3 days.
Ground: switch both cassettes to HEPES-buffered medium. Check that every well beats and record baseline video. Seal the cassettes and close the triple containment.
Late load into a large bay that is already powered at 37 C. Hold at 37 C through launch.
Launch. The bay logs temperature, acceleration and dose.
In orbit: first medium exchange. Record baseline brightfield video of all 24 wells (about 10-20 s each), with no arm motion during recording.
Daily video of all wells, plus calcium-reporter fluorescence video if a reporter line flies. Repeat every day to day 10.
Medium exchange (repeat on days 5, 7 and 9).
Mid-mission preservation: 2 wells into 4% PFA and 2 wells into RNA stabilizer. The bay cools these wells only if they sit in a separate cassette zone. Otherwise they stay at 37 C (see limitations).
Drug challenge: add the customer's test compound at 2 concentrations, 4 wells each, and vehicle to 4 wells. Record video before dosing and at about 30 min and 2 h after.
Medium exchange and final full video set. Optionally, the arm carries the bay to the central 40x microscope for close-up images of reporter cells.
End of lab operations: preserve 6 wells in PFA and 6 wells in RNA stabilizer. Keep the remaining 8 wells live at 37 C.
Re-entry and splashdown. The bay holds 37 C until handover to the courier on the recovery ship.

in_flight.name: Beat rate and beat-interval irregularity
in_flight.method: Brightfield video from the bay microscope, analysed with motion-vector analysis as in the CRS-9 study. The spread of beat intervals is the arrhythmia measure.

in_flight.name: Contraction and relaxation velocity (relative, not absolute force)
in_flight.method: The same brightfield video, using motion-vector analysis.

in_flight.name: Calcium transients (only if a calcium-reporter line flies)
in_flight.method: Fluorescence video on one of the bay microscope's 2 fluorescence channels. The usable kinetics depend on the camera frame rate.

in_flight.name: Acute response to the test compound
in_flight.method: Video before and after the fluidics adds the drug or vehicle, compared within the same wells.

in_flight.name: Cell coverage and morphology
in_flight.method: Brightfield images, with optional 40x images in the central lab microscope.

in_flight.name: Environment log
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure, humidity and acceleration sensors, plus the active silicon dosimeter and passive TLDs.

post_flight.name: Whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing
post_flight.method: RNA-stabilized wells from day 5 and day 10, compared with matched ground wells. Expected readouts are mitochondrial, calcium-handling and stress pathways.

post_flight.name: Sarcomere structure and cardiac markers
post_flight.method: Immunofluorescence on PFA-fixed wells (cardiac troponin T, alpha-actinin). Image analysis measures sarcomere length and organisation.

post_flight.name: Calcium handling and beating in live-return cells
post_flight.method: Calcium imaging and video contractility on the live wells, starting about 1-3 days after splashdown and repeated up to 10 days to follow recovery.

post_flight.name: Recovery transcriptome
post_flight.method: RNA from live-return wells about 10 days after return, as in the CRS-9 design.

post_flight.name: Spent-medium analysis
post_flight.method: Medium returned in the waste bag, tested with the customer's choice of assays (for example metabolites or released cardiac proteins).

sample_return.note: Live wells must stay at 37 C from the bay to the customer's lab. In CRS-20, live tissues were retrieved two days after splashdown and then hand-carried at 37 C and 5% CO2 to the lab, and they were still usable. LELP-1's plan (handover about 20 min after splashdown, then 1-2 days to the lab) is about 25-49 h, which is close to that heritage. It needs a portable 37 C incubator in the courier chain, and we set a target of 48 h or less. PFA-fixed wells should travel at 4 C. RNA-stabilized wells should travel at 4 C and be frozen at -80 C on arrival.

experiments.ground_control: Plate a second cassette from the same cell lot on the same day, with the same HEPES medium, reservoirs, gas-permeable lids and fluidics schedule. Run it in an identical bay on the ground, replaying the flight temperature log and the timing of every medium change, image, drug addition and preservation. If possible, also replay the launch and re-entry vibration and acceleration profiles. Give the live ground wells the same courier hold and the same post-flight analysis. Both heritage studies used matched ground controls. This design has no in-flight 1 g centrifuge control.

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source figure. We chose a large bay because its 24 wells allow replicates, drug arms and three end-points, and because the microscope plus fluidics need the mass margin. The medium volume assumes about 1 mL per well for 5 exchanges. Peak power is 29 W: up to about 18 W for the thermoelectric block holding 37 C, about 8 W for the microscope LED and camera, and about 3 W for the controller. This stays inside the 30 W large-bay limit only if pumps never run during imaging.

needs: Late load (live cells handed over about 24 h before launch) into a bay that is already powered and held at 37 C through launch, ascent and re-entry, up to handover on the recovery ship
An imaging schedule locked out against robotic-arm motion, because vibration corrupts beat analysis from video
A video frame rate high enough for beat timing and, if used, calcium transients (the customer sets the minimum; LumaScope-class default modes need checking)
Two thermal zones, or a second cassette, if fixed and RNA-stabilized wells are to be cooled to 4 C while live wells stay at 37 C
A portable 37 C incubator in the courier chain from ship to lab
Downlink budget for daily video of 24 wells, or on-board beat analysis that sends down only summary numbers and selected clips
limitations: Short exposure. The heritage flights lasted about 30 days (CRS-20) and 5.5 weeks (CRS-9), but a LELP-1 mission lasts 2-14 days and sees only early changes. Force loss and mitochondrial damage may not have time to develop. On CRS-9, the beat rate was similar to ground even after 2.5 weeks.

No absolute force. Video of 2D monolayers gives beat rate, timing and relative motion, not twitch force. Measuring force needs post-based engineered heart tissues with sensors, which the customer would have to supply and qualify.
No CO2. The heritage cultures ran at 5% CO2. LELP-1 uses HEPES-buffered medium, so ground controls must use the same medium, and results are not directly comparable with ISS data.

Cells cannot practically launch frozen. One major supplier specifies storage at -150 C (colder than the -80 C passive cassette), the thaw includes centrifugation, and cells are ready only from day 3. A live late load is therefore needed, which adds work in a lab at the launch site.

Culture length. The same supplier states cells can be kept for at least 14 days after thawing. This plan needs about 21 days from thaw to splashdown, plus post-flight work. The heritage cultures ran for more than 5 weeks, but the customer must confirm that their line stays stable for that long.
Beating and calcium kinetics depend strongly on temperature, so any thermal drift in the bay will confound the results.

All live-return samples carry launch and re-entry loads and 1-2 days at 1 g before reaching the lab. Cells readapt early (on CRS-9, gene expression reverted toward ground-like levels after return), so live-return results are partly recovery data.

The orbit is 550 km sun-synchronous, so the radiation dose differs from the ISS. Dosimeter data are logged, but radiation and microgravity effects cannot be separated without a 1 g centrifuge control in flight.
Few replicates per arm (4-8 wells) and possibly only one cell line per bay. Studying donor-to-donor variability, as in the 3-donor CRS-9 design, needs several bays.
No crew. Nobody can fix a well that stops beating, a bubble or a failed medium exchange.

experiments.title: Immune T-cell activation
experiments.why: Astronauts show immune dysregulation and reactivation of latent herpesviruses that last through 6-month ISS missions. On Earth, weak T-cell activation is also seen in older people. Since Spacelab 1 in 1983, flight experiments have found that human lymphocytes activated in suspension with the mitogen Con A respond much less in microgravity than on the ground. In a 2006 ISS study, gene expression already differed from the on-board 1 g control 1.5 hours after activation. Microgravity lets researchers weaken early T-cell activation without drugs or genetic edits, and study those early steps.
customers: University and hospital immunology labs studying T-cell signalling and immunosenescence (ageing of the immune system)
Space agency human-research programmes that need data on astronaut immune dysregulation and on countermeasures
Pharmaceutical and biotech groups testing immunomodulating compounds on a model where T-cell activation is already impaired
Research groups that already have ISS T-cell data and want a repeat flight with a different activator, donor set or time points

heritage.mission: Spacelab 1
heritage.what_flew: Cultures of human lymphocytes exposed to the mitogen concanavalin A (Con A) in orbit
heritage.finding: Activation was strongly depressed. The Science paper reports less than 3 percent of the activation seen in ground controls.

heritage.mission: First Spacelab Life Sciences mission (SLS-1)
heritage.what_flew: Lymphocytes and monocytes attached to microcarrier beads, activated with Con A
heritage.finding: With the cells attached to beads, DNA synthesis and interferon-gamma production more than doubled in microgravity. The authors concluded that the depression seen in earlier flights came from impaired macrophage function, not from a lymphocyte defect.

heritage.mission: Soyuz TMA-9 flight to the ISS; ESA KUBIK facility with LYCIS hardware
heritage.what_flew: Purified human T cells from four donors, launched unfrozen at about 16-22 C and activated in orbit with Con A plus anti-CD28 at 36.5 C. A 1 g centrifuge control ran on board at the same time. Activation was stopped with RNAlater after 1.5 h, and samples returned on a Soyuz landing on 28 September 2006.
heritage.finding: Microarrays found 47 genes down-regulated twofold or more in microgravity compared with the on-board 1 g control. These included immediate early genes such as TNF, EGR1 and EGR2. Targets of Rel/NF-kB, CREB and SRF were down-regulated, and cRel binding sites were the most common among the inhibited genes.

heritage.mission: T-Cell Activation in Aging (launched on SpaceX-3)
heritage.what_flew: Isolated human T cells in experiment containers. The crew used plungers to add an activator and then a fixative. Part of the samples ran at 1 g artificial gravity as a control.
heritage.finding: The NASA page we cite describes only the design. Its stated aim was to study the mechanisms of diminished T-cell activation in ageing and in astronauts. It gives no results.

protocol.sample: Human peripheral T cells (or PBMC, which keep the accessory cells) from 2 donors. Cells are cryopreserved before launch. They can be pre-labelled with a cell-tracking dye so proliferation can be measured after return.
protocol.container: Large bay 24-well cassette with gas-permeable lids and a filtered (about 0.4 um) outlet on each well, so supernatant can be drawn off without removing cells. Planned layout: 2 donors x 3 conditions (unstimulated; Con A + anti-CD28 to match the ISS heritage; soluble anti-CD3/anti-CD28) x 3 time points = 18 wells, plus 6 wells for imaging, viability and spares.
protocol.launch_state: cryopreserved (-80 C passive cassette); medium, activators and fixatives held in bay reservoirs
protocol.light_gas: No light needed (dark incubation; the microscope LEDs run only during imaging). No CO2 supply: HEPES-buffered RPMI-type medium in sealed wells with gas-permeable lids.

steps.action: Load the cryo cassette, reagent reservoirs (HEPES medium, Con A + anti-CD28, anti-CD3/anti-CD28, RNAlater, paraformaldehyde fixative) and the empty well cassette. Fix a pre-launch baseline aliquot of each donor on the ground.
Launch. Cells stay in the passive -80 C cassette. Bay reservoirs are held at 4 C.
Automated thaw at 37 C, then about 1:10 dilution into warm medium to lower the DMSO level, and dispensing into the wells. Brightfield images give the starting cell count and morphology.

After an 18-24 h rest at 37 C, fix one unstimulated set (t = 0) in RNAlater. Pump the activators into the stimulated wells. Lock out arm motion for the first 2 h. At 1.5 h, add RNAlater to the early-gene wells, as in the 2006 ISS flight.

24 h after activation: draw supernatant through the well filter into a sealed sample reservoir for cytokine analysis, then fix the cells with paraformaldehyde for flow cytometry (CD69, CD25). Take brightfield images of cell clustering every 6 h from day 2.
72 h after activation: split the final wells between paraformaldehyde (proliferation, Ki-67 or dye dilution) and RNAlater. Image all wells. Set the bay to 4 C.
Bay held at 4 C through re-entry and splashdown. Fixed cassette and supernatant reservoir are handed to the customer's courier at 4 C.

in_flight.name: Cell number, morphology and clustering (activated T cells form clusters)
in_flight.method: Brightfield time-lapse with the bay's LumaScope-class microscope, every 6 h from thaw to the last fixation

in_flight.name: Post-thaw viability
in_flight.method: Two-colour live/dead fluorescent stain pumped into the dedicated imaging wells and read on the 2 fluorescence channels

in_flight.name: Closer look at selected wells
in_flight.method: Robotic arm moves the bay to the central 40x fluorescence microscope, outside the activation and fixation windows

in_flight.name: Exact activation and fixation times
in_flight.method: Time-tagged fluidics valve and pump log

in_flight.name: Thermal, radiation and acceleration history
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure and humidity sensors, active silicon dosimeter plus passive TLDs, and the accelerometer log (to flag any fixation that happened during arm motion)

post_flight.name: Immediate early gene expression (for example EGR1, EGR2, TNF) and later activation genes (IL2, IFNG, IL2RA)
post_flight.method: RNA extraction from RNAlater-fixed wells, then RNA-seq or microarray, with qPCR confirmation

post_flight.name: Activation surface markers (CD69, CD25) and proliferation (Ki-67 or tracking-dye dilution)
post_flight.method: Flow cytometry on paraformaldehyde-fixed cells

post_flight.name: Secreted cytokines (IL-2, IFN-gamma, TNF)
post_flight.method: Multiplex immunoassay on the filtered 24 h supernatants (4 C stability needs ground validation first)

post_flight.name: Pathway activity (for example Rel/NF-kB, CREB and SRF targets)
post_flight.method: Analysis of transcription-factor binding sites and pathways in the gene-expression data, compared with the ground control and, if flown, the 1 g centrifuge control

sample_return.note: All cells are chemically fixed in orbit, so nothing needs to come back alive. The manufacturer states RNAlater stabilises RNA for 1 month at 4 C (and indefinitely at -20 C), which easily covers the return. The 144 h limit is our estimate and is set by the unfrozen 24 h supernatants: drawn on day 3, they spend about 4 days in orbit, then about 20 min to courier pickup and 1-2 days in transit, so about 6 days at 4 C. The last paraformaldehyde-fixed cells (day 5) reach the lab after about 3-4 days. The bay cannot go below 4 C, so supernatants cannot be frozen in orbit; their cytokine stability for 6 days at 4 C must be checked on the ground before flight. Keep everything at 4 C in transit and avoid temperatures above 25 C.

experiments.ground_control: Synchronous ground control: an identical flight-model bay and cassette loaded with the same donor cell lots and reagent batches. It replays the same timeline (offset by a few hours) and the recorded flight temperature profile, including the -80 C hold, thaw, 37 C phases and the 4 C return hold. If possible, it also gets a launch vibration profile on a shaker table. Add a pre-launch baseline fixed on the ground. The key flight control in the 2006 and 2014 ISS studies was an on-board 1 g centrifuge running at the same time in KUBIK, which separates microgravity from radiation, launch and handling effects. LELP-1 should fly one (see needs). Without it, the result is flight versus ground only. Because the 2006 flight launched live cells unfrozen, the cryopreserved-launch step should also be checked against fresh cells on the ground.
