Passive -80 C cryo cassette with donor cell vials
Filled reagent reservoirs (medium, two activator mixes, RNAlater, paraformaldehyde, live/dead stain) plus sealed supernatant reservoir
Fluidics: micro-pumps, valves, manifold, tubing
LumaScope-class inverted microscope (brightfield + 2 fluorescence channels)
Bay electronics, sensor harness, mounting and containment liners

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source claim. A large bay is needed because the planned 2-donor x 3-condition x 3-time-point layout plus imaging wells uses all 24 wells, and the separate reagent and supernatant reservoirs do not fit a medium bay's 3.3 kg. The 5.6 kg total stays under the 6.0 kg limit. Peak power: 25 W thermoelectric block (heating to 37 C at thaw, cooling to 4 C at the end) plus about 3 W for the pumps = 28 W, under the 30 W limit. The microscope is scheduled only when pumps are idle and the thermoelectric block is in steady hold. Component masses are allocations, to be replaced by measured values from the team.

needs: In-flight 1 g centrifuge control (not part of the standard bay): a second identical cassette on a small rotor. At 5 cm radius, 1 g needs about 134 rpm. Without it, the core control from the ISS heritage is missing.
Filtered well outlets and a sealed supernatant reservoir, so medium can be harvested in microgravity without drawing up the cells
Arm-motion lockout (keeping the vehicle in the 1e-6 g regime) for about 2 h after activator addition and during each fixation
A -80 C passive cassette hold time that covers the launch campaign plus 1 day in orbit, with the cassette temperature logged
Fixation events time-stamped against the accelerometer and dosimeter logs
limitations: Without the added 1 g centrifuge, LELP-1 cannot tell microgravity effects apart from launch, radiation and handling effects. The 2006 and 2014 ISS studies used this control.

LELP-1 has no crew and no way to pellet cells. Thawed cells are diluted rather than washed, so some DMSO stays in the medium. Medium changes must go through filters, and activator or fixative mixing relies on pumped flow because there is no sedimentation or convection.

Bead-based activators need bead-cell contact, which in microgravity depends on mixing. The protocol therefore uses soluble activators (Con A + anti-CD28, soluble anti-CD3/CD28). Results with bead activation are not directly comparable.
Cell attachment changes the outcome: on SLS-1, bead-attached lymphocytes and monocytes responded more in microgravity, not less. Results from suspension wells apply to suspension culture only.
There is no CO2 supply. HEPES-buffered medium in sealed wells can drift in pH over several days of activated, high-metabolism culture, so 72 h is about the practical limit without a medium exchange.
No in-flight flow cytometry, cytokine assay or RNA readout. In flight, the satellite only gives images and environment logs; the molecular answers come after return.
Supernatants cannot be frozen (the bay minimum is 4 C), so cytokine values depend on about 6 days of stability at 4 C.
A 2-14 day free-flyer studies isolated cells in vitro. It cannot reproduce astronaut immune changes in the body over months, latent virus reactivation, stress hormones or the role of other tissues.
Few donors per flight (2 planned), so donor-to-donor variability limits the statistics. Several flights or more donors in a second bay may be needed.
The radiation environment at 550 km sun-synchronous orbit differs from the ISS, so dose comparisons with ISS heritage data need the on-board dosimeter record.

corrections_to_leads: Cogoli et al., Science 1984: the paper is 'Cell sensitivity to gravity' by Cogoli A, Tschopp A, Fuchs-Bislin P, Science 225:228-230. Its abstract says lymphocytes reached 'less than 3 percent of the activation of ground controls'. The abstract does not name the mission. The link to Spacelab 1 (1983) comes from the ESA SP-1206 page. We dropped 'STS-9' because no opened source gives it.

Chang et al., J Leukoc Biol 2012: the flight activator was Con A plus anti-CD28, not anti-CD3/CD28. Anti-CD3/anti-CD28 beads were used only in the ground-based simulated-microgravity studies. Only purified T cells from four donors flew, not peripheral blood leukocytes. They launched unfrozen at about 16-22 C on Soyuz TMA-9 (18 September 2006), ran in ESA's KUBIK facility with LYCIS hardware, were activated for 1.5 h, stopped with RNAlater, and returned on a Soyuz landing on 28 September 2006. The on-board 1 g centrifuge control is confirmed. Cogoli was a co-author.
Chang et al. 2012 names Rel/NF-kB, CREB and SRF targets as down-regulated, with cRel binding sites the most common. Calling Rel/NF-kB the single 'main pathway' oversimplifies it.

SLS-1 (1991): the bead-attached cells were lymphocytes and monocytes together (ESA SP-1206), and they responded more in microgravity, not less. A blanket statement that all flown T cells respond less is wrong.
Some web summaries say Spacelab 1 activation was 'depressed by nearly 90%'. We could not confirm that figure from a primary source and did not use it.

Martinez et al. 2015 (Hughes-Fulford lab, STS-131) is not an in-orbit activation study. Mice flew for 15 days, and their splenocytes were activated on the ground about 2.5 h after landing. We left it out of the heritage list for this reason.
Some secondary sources say stratospheric balloon flights ruled out cosmic radiation as the cause. We did not confirm this in an opened primary source and left it out.

experiments.title: Bone cells: resorption and mineralization
experiments.why: On Earth, osteoporosis comes from an imbalance between osteoclasts, which remove bone, and osteoblasts, which build it. In space this imbalance appears quickly: astronauts lose bone mineral density at about 1-1.5% per month in weight-bearing bones. Flight experiments show that isolated bone cells respond to microgravity directly. Osteoclasts resorbed more bone in flight, osteoblasts grew more slowly, and cultured fetal mouse bones mineralized less. A sealed, automated bay lets a lab test this cell-level response, and drugs or materials that might correct it, without crew time.
customers: Pharmaceutical and biotech groups developing anti-resorptive or bone-anabolic drugs who want an unloaded cell model
Academic bone and mechanobiology labs studying how osteoclasts and osteoblasts sense gravity
Space agency human research programmes working on astronaut bone loss countermeasures
Bone-graft and resorbable biomaterial companies testing how cells resorb or mineralize their scaffolds
Dental and craniofacial research groups using dentin or bone substrates

heritage.mission: FOTON-M3 (experiments OSTEO, OCLAST, PITS)
heritage.platform: Free-flyer satellite (recoverable Foton capsule, 12 days in orbit)
heritage.what_flew: OSTEO: osteoclast precursors on a synthetic bone-like biomaterial (skelite) in perfusion bioreactors for 10 days. OCLAST and PITS: differentiated osteoclasts on devitalized bovine bone slices for 4 days. Ground replicates in the same bioreactors; OCLAST also had an in-flight centrifuge control.
heritage.finding: Genes for osteoclast maturation and activity rose severalfold versus ground controls. More collagen telopeptides were released than in ground and centrifuge controls, showing increased bone resorption. The authors concluded that osteoclasts and their precursors are direct targets of microgravity.

heritage.mission: STS-56 (Space Shuttle Discovery)
heritage.what_flew: MC3T3-E1 mouse osteoblasts launched quiescent in 0.5% fetal calf serum, activated in flight with fresh 10% serum medium, and fixed 4 days later before return. Ground controls ran in parallel in identical equipment.
heritage.finding: Flight osteoblasts grew slowly (55 vs 141 cells per microscopic field), had fewer actin stress fibres, and had nuclei 30% smaller and oblong. Total glucose use and PGE2 synthesis were lower because there were fewer cells; per cell they were comparable, so viability was normal.

heritage.mission: Bion-10 (Cosmos-2229)
heritage.what_flew: 17-day-old fetal mouse metatarsal long bones cultured for 4 days at 37 C in automated plunger boxes, fixed automatically with formaldehyde, with an in-flight 1 g control on the Biobox centrifuge.
heritage.finding: Mineralization of the diaphysis was modest in all groups, and significantly lower in microgravity than in the in-flight 1 g control.

heritage.mission: IML-2 on STS-65
heritage.what_flew: 17-day-old fetal mouse metatarsals in gas-permeable culture bags for 4 days at 37 C, fixed in flight with glutaraldehyde; groups given 3, 6 or 12 h of 1 g per day on the on-board centrifuge, plus constant 1 g and microgravity groups.
heritage.finding: Overall bone length was unaffected, but proteoglycan content and the length increase of the mineralized diaphysis were reduced in microgravity. Daily 1 g for at least 6 h abolished the reduction in cartilage mineralization.

protocol.sample: Two arms in one cassette (our design). Arm A, resorption: an osteoclast precursor line (for example murine RAW 264.7) or human CD14+ monocytes, seeded onto devitalized bovine cortical bone slices or dentin discs, plus calcium-phosphate-coated clear wells for in-flight imaging. Arm B, early mineralization: MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts on clear tissue-culture wells.
protocol.container: Large bay 24-well cassette: 8 wells bone/dentin slices (Arm A), 4 wells calcium-phosphate-coated clear wells (Arm A, imaged), 8 wells clear plastic (Arm B), 4 wells cell-free slices and coated wells as background controls. Gas-permeable lids inside the sealed BSL-2 bay.
protocol.launch_state: Cryopreserved (cells in freezing medium in the -80 C passive cassette); slices and coated wells launch dry and sterile; media and reagents in reservoirs. Labile factors (RANKL, M-CSF, ascorbate) need 4 C storage while the bay runs at 37 C (see needs).
protocol.light_gas: Dark except during imaging. No CO2: HEPES-buffered alpha-MEM based media, sealed bay air headspace through gas-permeable lids.

steps.action: Launch and orbit insertion. Cells stay frozen in the passive cassette; bay held at 4 C.
Automated thaw, dilution and wash; seed Arm A onto slices and coated wells, Arm B onto clear wells. Bay ramps to 37 C. Brightfield image of all clear wells to record seeding density.
Medium exchange. Arm A: add RANKL (plus M-CSF if primary monocytes). Arm B: growth medium. Collect first supernatant aliquot from each well.
Arm A medium plus RANKL refreshed. Arm B switched to osteogenic medium (ascorbic acid and beta-glycerophosphate) once near confluence. Daily brightfield imaging begins for fusion and spreading.
Medium exchange in both arms; supernatant aliquot saved for collagen telopeptide (for example CTX-I) and TRAP5b assays after return. Imaging: count multinucleated cells on coated wells.
Medium exchange; add calcein to Arm B medium to label newly deposited mineral. Supernatant aliquot saved. Brightfield imaging of coated wells for cleared areas; calcein fluorescence on Arm B.
Medium exchange; supernatant aliquot saved. Full imaging pass of all clear wells; optional robotic-arm transfer to the central 40x fluorescence microscope.

Final supernatant collection. Half of each arm fixed with buffered paraformaldehyde (for TRAP, actin, pit and mineral staining); the other half covered with an RNA-stabilizing reagent. Bay ramps to 4 C straight away.
Fixative replaced with buffer at 4 C. Bay stays at 4 C through de-orbit, re-entry and splashdown.

in_flight.name: Seeding density and attachment
in_flight.method: Brightfield imaging of clear and coated wells on day 1 and day 2

in_flight.name: Osteoclast fusion (multinucleated cells)
in_flight.method: Daily brightfield imaging of calcium-phosphate-coated clear wells; count large multinucleated cells

in_flight.name: Resorption areas
in_flight.method: Brightfield imaging of cleared areas in the calcium-phosphate coating, days 6 to 11, where contrast allows

in_flight.name: New mineral deposition (Arm B)
in_flight.method: Calcein fluorescence (green channel) after calcein is added on day 8

in_flight.name: Higher-resolution cell morphology
in_flight.method: Optional robotic-arm transfer to the central 40x fluorescence microscope

in_flight.name: Culture environment
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure, humidity, seal status and acceleration logs; dose from the active silicon dosimeter and passive TLDs

post_flight.name: Bone resorption pit area and depth
post_flight.method: Remove cells from bone/dentin slices, stain (for example toluidine blue) and image by light microscopy, or by SEM/profilometry

post_flight.name: Collagen breakdown released into medium
post_flight.method: Collagen telopeptide assay (for example CTX-I ELISA) on saved supernatants; FOTON-M3 measured collagen telopeptide release as its resorption readout

post_flight.name: Osteoclast number and maturity
post_flight.method: TRAP staining of fixed wells; count TRAP-positive multinucleated cells; TRAP5b in supernatants

post_flight.name: Cytoskeleton and sealing zones
post_flight.method: Phalloidin (actin) and nuclear staining of fixed wells; confocal imaging

post_flight.name: Osteoclast and osteoblast gene expression
post_flight.method: RT-qPCR or RNA-seq of stabilized samples (for example Acp5, Ctsk, Mmp9, Nfatc1, Calcr; Runx2, Sp7, Alpl, Col1a1, Bglap)

post_flight.name: Osteoblast differentiation and mineral
post_flight.method: Alkaline phosphatase activity or staining; Alizarin Red S staining and extraction for calcium deposit quantification

sample_return.note: All wells are fixed or RNA-stabilized in orbit on day 11, so no live cells need to survive re-entry. Keep the cassette at 4 C from day 11 through recovery and courier transfer (about 20 min after splashdown plus 1-2 days to the lab), which can total about 3 to 6 days. The 168 h limit is our estimate: the RNA-stabilizing reagent maker rates RNA as stable for 1 month at 4 C, but supernatant proteins are less certain. If the total will exceed 168 h, put stabilized samples and supernatants on dry ice or at -80 C on the recovery ship. Fixed slices tolerate longer at 4 C once fixative is replaced with buffer.

experiments.ground_control: An identical flight-model module and 24-well cassette, filled from the same cell vials, slice batch and reagent lots, runs on the ground in a spare bay. It replays the flight temperature log and the same fluidics and imaging timeline, offset by a few hours so it can follow the actual flight events. Fixed and stabilized samples are handled and shipped the same way. A synchronous 1 g in-flight centrifuge control, as flown on FOTON-M3 (OCLAST), Bion-10 and IML-2, is the best way to separate microgravity from launch and radiation effects but is not part of the standard bay.

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source claim. Large bay chosen because the two-arm design needs 24 wells, eight reservoirs and a microscope; 5.9 kg is under the 6.0 kg limit. Peak power of about 28 W (under 30 W) assumes the thermoelectric block holding 37 C (about 12 W), microscope LED and camera (about 8 W), pumps and valves during a medium exchange (about 5 W) and controller (about 3 W) at the same time. The 4-to-37 C ramp, the 37-to-4 C ramp and the thaw are scheduled when the microscope is off. Item masses are scaled from typical small lab hardware and must be confirmed with a prototype.

Passive -80 C cryo-cassette for cell vials at launch
Fluidics: micro-pumps, valves, manifold, thaw and seeding lines
Reservoirs filled: two media, RANKL/M-CSF, osteogenic supplements, calcein, fixative, RNA-stabilizing reagent, PBS, waste
LumaScope-class inverted microscope (brightfield + 2 fluorescence channels) with XY stage
Supernatant aliquot rack (about 100 small tubes)
Bay sensors, harness and controller board
Module frame and mounting

needs: Optional 1 g reference centrifuge for a subset of wells, so microgravity can be separated from launch and radiation effects
Cold (4 C) zone for labile factors and supernatant aliquots during the 37 C culture; the bay's single thermoelectric setpoint cannot hold 37 C and 4 C at once
Brightfield and fluorescence imaging time on the microscope schedule every day from day 1 to day 11
Optional robotic-arm slot on the central 40x fluorescence microscope on day 10
Recovery-ship -80 C freezer or dry ice for stabilized samples and supernatants if transit to the lab will exceed about 168 h
limitations: Bone and dentin slices are opaque, so resorption pits on them cannot be seen with the inverted microscope in flight; only the calcium-phosphate-coated clear wells give in-flight resorption data, and their contrast in brightfield may be weak until they are stained after return.

Mature mineralized nodules from osteoblast lines usually need longer culture than a 14-day mission allows (our assumption), so Arm B gives early mineralization and differentiation markers, not mature mineralized matrix.
The flight evidence for reduced mineralization comes from fetal mouse bone organ cultures, not from osteoblast monolayers; Arm B tests whether a similar effect shows up in a simpler cell model.
Cells must be thawed and seeded in orbit; thaw and attachment losses add variability, and the protocol must be proven on the ground first.
Without the optional centrifuge, launch loads, radiation at 550 km and handling in the bay cannot be fully separated from microgravity; the ground control covers only temperature and timeline.
Isolated cells on slices lack osteocytes, blood supply, hormones and mechanical loading, so results show direct cell responses, not whole-skeleton bone loss.
No crew means no slice replacement, no fresh-reagent preparation and no extra fixation time points beyond those planned in the reservoirs.
Microgravity is about 1e-4 to 1e-3 g while the robotic arm moves; arm moves should be avoided during the key fusion and resorption days.
Samples reach the lab 1-2 days after splashdown, so no live-cell work after return is possible; everything is fixed or stabilized in orbit.

corrections_to_leads: Tamma et al. 2009 is correct (FASEB J 23(8):2549-2554, FOTON-M3, 2007, a free-flying recoverable capsule). The lead mixes two set-ups: the 10-day OSTEO run put osteoclast precursors on a synthetic bone-like material (skelite) in perfusion bioreactors. Differentiated osteoclasts on devitalized bovine bone slices (OCLAST, PITS) ran for only 4 days. No dentin was used.
Hughes-Fulford and Lewis, Exp Cell Res 1996 (224:103-109) is correct, but the osteoblasts flew on STS-56 (Discovery) in April 1993; 1996 is the publication year.
The 'about 10 days, 37 C' protocol in the lead is our own LELP-1 design. It does not copy any one flight. The flight cultures that used bone slices or fixed osteoblasts ran for 4 days.

Mineralization heritage comes from organ-cultured fetal mouse metatarsals on Bion-10 (Cosmos-2229, 29 Dec 1992 to 10 Jan 1993) and IML-2 on STS-65 (July 1994) (van Loon et al. 2024), not from osteoblast monolayers. The 3, 6 and 12 h daily 1 g groups flew on IML-2 only; Bion-10 had a microgravity group and a 1 g centrifuge control.
FOTON-M3 measured collagen telopeptides released into the medium; the paper abstract does not name a CTX-I ELISA, so that assay choice is ours.

experiments.title: C. elegans muscle and ageing
experiments.why: Astronauts lose muscle in orbit, and people on Earth lose muscle with age, disuse and diseases such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The worm C. elegans grows from larva to adult in about four days, has well-mapped genetics, and has been studied in space for more than 20 years. On ISS flights, worms grown in microgravity had less myosin heavy chain, smaller body-wall muscle cells and less strength, and similar gene changes appeared across missions. An uncrewed free-flyer could repeat these runs more often, without waiting for crew time, to test which genes and drugs protect muscle.
customers: University C. elegans and muscle biology groups studying spaceflight muscle loss and ageing
Space agency life-science and astronaut countermeasure programmes
Pharma and biotech teams screening drugs against muscle wasting, sarcopenia or muscular dystrophy in a whole animal
Companies that make C. elegans phenotyping tools (for example microfluidic strength or imaging assays) and want flight data

heritage.mission: ICE-First (International C. elegans Experiment First), flown during the ESA DELTA mission
heritage.platform: ISS (carried on a Soyuz that docked with the ISS)
heritage.what_flew: Mixed-stage wild-type and transgenic C. elegans in chemically defined medium (CeMM) in gas-permeable culture bags inside a vented Biorack experiment container. Worms spent 2 days at 12 C in transit, then 9 days on the ISS at 20 C, and were frozen in liquid nitrogen within 2 h of landing.
heritage.finding: Myosin heavy chain fell in body-wall and pharyngeal muscle, with lower expression of the myogenic factors HLH-1, PEB-1, CEH-22 and PHA-4. Flown worms moved more slowly after return. A later analysis of the same flight found fewer polyglutamine (Q35::YFP) aggregates in body-wall muscle, and seven genes down-regulated in space extended lifespan when inactivated on the ground.

heritage.mission: CERISE (C. elegans RNA Interference in Space Experiment), JAXA
heritage.platform: ISS Japanese Experiment Module, Cell Biology Experiment Facility; up on Space Shuttle Atlantis STS-129 (16 November 2009), down on Space Shuttle Endeavour STS-130 (21 February 2010)
heritage.what_flew: Synchronised L1 larvae held in stasis in M9C buffer, then given bacterial food on the ISS (start 20 November 2009) and grown 4 days at 20 C in microgravity and on a 1 G centrifuge. Movies were downlinked. Samples were frozen at -80 C in the ISS freezer (MELFI) and returned.
heritage.finding: Gene and protein levels for muscle thick filaments, cytoskeleton and mitochondrial enzymes fell in microgravity worms compared with the 1 G centrifuge worms. Swimming frequency differed, body length was about 5.5% shorter, and fat storage was lower.

heritage.mission: Molecular Muscle Experiment (MME), University of Nottingham with Exeter and Lancaster
heritage.platform: ISS (launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9, 5 December 2018)
heritage.what_flew: Wild-type N2 and unc-70 mutant worms (the strains used in the muscle analysis), about 500 synchronised L1 larvae per polyethylene bag in 6.5 mL with freeze-dried E. coli OP50. Bags were cold-stowed at 8-13 C until arrival, incubated 5 days on the ISS, then frozen at -80 C. The project also used gene changes and drugs.
heritage.finding: Ground tests for the hardware showed that gas exchange limits worm growth in sealed plastic bags, with best growth at 5-7 mL (MME bags about 8.4 cm2/mL surface area to volume; ICE-First bags about 10 cm2/mL). In flight worms, the ratio of body-wall muscle length to body length was 29.7% lower in wild type and 27.4% lower in unc-70.

heritage.mission: NIS (Neural Integration System), JAXA
heritage.year: Not stated in the sources we checked
heritage.platform: ISS, with an on-board 1 G centrifuge control
heritage.what_flew: About 200 synchronised wild-type L1 larvae per sample in M9 buffer with cholesterol and E. coli food, grown at 20 C for 12 days in total. FUdR (75 uM) was added to stop new offspring. The astronaut fixed half of each sample in 0.7% paraformaldehyde at day 1 and day 10 of adulthood. Samples were kept at 4 C.
heritage.finding: Supported the MME result: wild-type body-wall muscle cell area was 23.4% smaller in microgravity than in the space 1 G control.

heritage.mission: micro-16
heritage.platform: ISS (launched on Northrop Grumman NG-15, 20 February 2021)
heritage.what_flew: Wild-type and dys-1 (BZ33, a Duchenne model) worms in FEP bags, from cultures kept in chemically defined medium (CeMM), handed over at 15 C and grown at 20 C on the ISS. Strength was measured in the second generation: crew loaded worms, including adults, into NemaFlex-S micropillar devices and recorded 1-minute videos. Bags were frozen at -80 C in MELFI for transcript analysis.
heritage.finding: Strength was 16.6% lower in flight worms than in ground controls. In flight, dys-1 worms were 23% weaker than wild-type worms. Transcripts showed more stress-response activity, lower mitochondrial and cytoskeletal activity, and links to neuronal calcium and acetylcholine signalling.

protocol.sample: C. elegans hermaphrodites: wild-type N2 plus one muscle-relevant strain chosen by the customer, for example dys-1 (BZ33), a body-wall muscle GFP reporter, or the Q35::YFP polyglutamine line. Each well holds about 50-100 age-synchronised L1 larvae.
protocol.container: 24-well gas-permeable culture cassette (about 0.5 mL liquid per well, thin gas-permeable film lid) inside the sealed bay. Two identical large modules fly: Module A (young-adult time point) and Module B (aged time point). Each bay block holds only one temperature, so the two time points need separate bays.
protocol.launch_state: Live, starved L1 larvae arrested in buffer (M9 with cholesterol) without food, held at 12 C. CERISE used a similar approach: L1 larvae held in stasis in buffer, then fed on orbit to start the experiment.
protocol.light_gas: Dark, except for short LED pulses during imaging. Air headspace through the gas-permeable lid in the sealed bay; no CO2 needed. Worm number and liquid volume are kept low because MME ground tests found gas exchange limits growth in sealed bags.

steps.action: Ground: bleach gravid adults, hatch eggs overnight in buffer to get synchronised L1 larvae, load each well, seal the cassettes, close the triple containment. Load reservoirs: freeze-dried E. coli OP50 food, FUdR, paraformaldehyde fixative, RNA preservation solution. Hold at 12 C.
Launch. Both modules hold 12 C; larvae stay arrested without food.

After orbit checkout and once the arm is parked (quasi-steady microgravity), raise both modules to 20 C. Pump bacterial food into every well to start development. Take baseline brightfield images of each well.
Daily, both modules: 30-60 s brightfield video per well (swimming frequency, body length, stage); fluorescence images if a reporter strain flies. Downlink a compressed subset.
Worms near L4: add FUdR to both modules (NIS used 75 uM) to stop new offspring before egg laying starts. Top up food.

Module A (about day 1 of adulthood): final video and fluorescence imaging. Then fix 12 wells with paraformaldehyde (for muscle staining and body length) and fill 12 wells with RNA preservation solution (for gene expression). Drop Module A to 4 C and hold it there until the courier hands it over.
Module B: top up food and FUdR. Continue daily imaging. Repeat every 2-3 days.
Module B (about day 9 of adulthood): final video and fluorescence imaging. Fix 12 wells and preserve 12 wells for RNA, as in Module A. Drop Module B to 4 C.
Deorbit and splashdown with both modules at 4 C. Recovery ship hands the sealed modules to the customer's courier (about 20 min after splashdown); cold transport at 4 C to the lab (about 1-2 days).

in_flight.name: Swimming (thrashing) frequency and wave shape
in_flight.method: Brightfield video from the bay's inverted microscope, tracked frame by frame. CERISE measured swimming from downlinked movies.

in_flight.name: Body length and developmental stage
in_flight.method: Brightfield images per well, measured with image analysis. CERISE found body length about 5.5% shorter in microgravity.

in_flight.name: Population and survival per well
in_flight.method: Count moving and still worms from video; check for contamination or starvation.

in_flight.name: Muscle reporter fluorescence or polyglutamine aggregates
in_flight.method: Bay fluorescence channel for a GFP or YFP muscle reporter. Aggregate counts and muscle cell detail need the 40x central microscope, reached by moving the bay with the arm.

in_flight.name: Environment log
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure, humidity and acceleration sensors; active silicon dosimeter and passive TLDs for radiation dose.

post_flight.name: Body-wall muscle cell area and muscle-to-body-length ratio
post_flight.method: Phalloidin staining of fixed worms and fluorescence microscopy, as in the MME and NIS analysis

post_flight.name: Myosin heavy chain and other muscle protein levels
post_flight.method: Quantitative western blot or mass-spectrometry proteomics, as in ICE-First and CERISE

post_flight.name: Gene expression (myogenic factors, mitochondrial, cytoskeletal, synaptic and longevity genes)
post_flight.method: RNA sequencing or qPCR on RNA-preserved wells, compared with the ground control

post_flight.name: Young versus aged comparison
post_flight.method: Compare Module A (day 1 adult) with Module B (about day 9 adult), flight against ground, for muscle structure and transcripts

post_flight.name: Polyglutamine aggregate count (if Q35::YFP flies)
post_flight.method: Fluorescence microscopy count of aggregates per worm, as in the ICE-First follow-up analysis

post_flight.name: Radiation dose
post_flight.method: TLD readout to report the total dose the worms received

sample_return.note: Fixed and RNA-preserved worms return sealed at 4 C. Module A samples are about 9 days past preservation at splashdown and about 10-11 days by the time they reach the lab. The 336 h (14 day) window is OUR ESTIMATE, and the customer must check it on the ground for both the fixative and the RNA solution. Heritage flights froze worms for gene and protein work: liquid nitrogen within 2 h of landing on ICE-First, and -80 C on orbit on CERISE, MME and micro-16. Only the NIS morphology samples were PFA-fixed and held at 4 C. If live worms are wanted for after-flight motility or lifespan tests, an extra well set must return unfixed at 15-20 C and reach the lab within about 48 h; this is also our estimate.

experiments.ground_control: Two identical ground modules with the same worm batches, food, reservoirs and cassette lots, run in a flight-like bay. Each step follows the flight timeline, with the bay's recorded temperature profile replayed about 1-2 days behind the flight (micro-16 replicated the flight temperature profile on a two-day delay). Ground modules are fixed, preserved, chilled and shipped the same way. This control cannot separate microgravity from space radiation or launch and re-entry loads. That needs an in-flight 1 G centrifuge control, as flown on CERISE and NIS.

module.basis: OUR ESTIMATE, per module (two identical L modules fly). To be conservative, the module mass includes the microscope, stage, fluidics and housing: 5.6 kg against the 6.0 kg limit. No crew, so the micro-16 strength assay (crew loaded worms into micropillar devices) cannot be repeated as flown; strength would need a new automated chip

The bay microscope is low magnification; sarcomere and mitochondrial detail needs the 40x central microscope or post-flight staining

About 2 h to hand-over and 1-2 days to the lab means live worms partly readapt to 1 g before any post-flight motility test

corrections_to_leads: Higashibata et al. 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:3209-3218) is confirmed; the title says 'myogenic transcription factors'. The paper says ICE-First flew during the ESA DELTA mission on a Soyuz to the ISS and calls it a 10-day spaceflight. Honda et al. 2012 gives 2 days at 12 C plus 9 days on the ISS at 20 C. The cited sources do not support the '10.9-day round trip', '53 independent samples' or 'April' details from the earlier draft, so these were removed.

Honda et al., Sci Rep 2012 (2:487) used ICE-First worms, not CERISE. It found fewer Q35::YFP polyglutamine aggregates in body-wall muscle, and seven down-regulated genes that extended lifespan on the ground when inactivated.

JAXA CERISE is confirmed: launched on Atlantis STS-129 on 16 November 2009, culture started on 20 November 2009, 4 days at 20 C in microgravity versus a 1 G centrifuge, frozen at -80 C, returned on Endeavour STS-130 on 21 February 2010 (Higashibata et al., npj Microgravity 2016).

MME (ISS, 2018) is confirmed: a Falcon 9 launch on 5 December 2018. MME worms ate freeze-dried E. coli OP50, not chemically defined medium. Kim et al. 2023 describes about 500 L1 per bag in 6.5 mL, cold stowage at 8-13 C, 5 days on the ISS, then -80 C. The '5000 L1 in 6 mL' figure is from the hardware-test work in Pollard et al. 2020. The 10 cm2/mL surface-to-volume ratio was ICE-First's; MME bags were about 8.4 cm2/mL. MME used no FUdR.

NIS reported muscle cell area for wild-type worms only (23.4% smaller in microgravity than in the space 1 G control). The unc-70 result (muscle-to-body-length ratio 27.4% lower) is from MME. NIS used 75 uM FUdR; we found no source for '40 uM'.

The 2023 strength-loss paper (Soni et al., Cells 2023, 16.6% weaker) comes from the micro-16 payload (NG-15, 20 February 2021), not from MME. The 23% figure compares dys-1 with wild-type worms on the ISS.

'Worms in liquid culture at about 20 C' is correct for all the flights checked. Return on the heritage flights was by freezing (liquid nitrogen after landing, or -80 C on orbit). Only NIS used paraformaldehyde fixation with 4 C storage.

experiments.title: 3D tumour spheroids for drug testing
experiments.why: Most early cancer drug tests use flat (2D) cell layers. Gene expression in 3D spheroids is much closer to clinical profiles than in 2D, so spheroids are a better model for drug screening. In microgravity, cancer cells can gather into 3D spheroids on their own, without a scaffold, as human thyroid cancer cells did on Shenzhou-8 in 2011 and on the ISS in 2017-2018. NASA has also run an ISS investigation of antibody-drug conjugates on cancer cells in microgravity. A recoverable free-flyer lets a customer grow these spheroids, dose them with a drug, fix them in orbit, and compare them with an identical ground control.
customers: Pharmaceutical and biotech oncology discovery groups testing small molecules or antibody-drug conjugates on 3D tumour models
Contract research organisations that offer 3D spheroid drug screening
Academic cancer biology and gravitational biology labs studying 3D growth, adhesion and signalling
Space agencies and research funders with cancer and microgravity programmes

heritage.mission: Shenzhou-8 with the German SIMBOX facility (Sino-German)
heritage.platform: Recoverable capsule (uncrewed Shenzhou-8 spacecraft, 17-day mission, landed 17 November 2011)
heritage.what_flew: FTC-133 human follicular thyroid cancer cells in an automated culture unit with two reserve tanks (medium and fixative) and a pump for fluid exchange. Medium was exchanged after 5 days in space and cells were fixed after 10 days. The hardware materials were tested not to inactivate RNAlater.
heritage.finding: Scaffold-free formation of extraordinarily large 3D aggregates, with altered expression of the EGF and CTGF genes. A later paper from the same group reports that the returned spheroids were 5-10 mm across, larger than spheroids usually made on Earth with a random positioning machine.

heritage.mission: CellBox-2 (launched on SpaceX CRS-13)
heritage.platform: ISS (launched 15 December 2017 on Falcon 9 / Dragon, cells returned 12 January 2018)
heritage.what_flew: FTC-133 thyroid cancer cells in six automated hardware units with PEEK culture chambers, automatic medium exchange and fixation. Cells were cultured at 28 C on the ISS. Five days after launch the medium was changed in all six units and three units were fixed. The other three were fixed five days later. Fixed cells were stored at 4 C.
heritage.finding: Multicellular spheroids formed in all spaceflight units. VCL, PXN, ITGB1, RELA, ERK1 and ERK2 mRNA were significantly lower than in ground controls. The response to microgravity was mainly anti-proliferative. The same paper reports that no spheroids formed in the earlier CellBox-1 mission, where cells had grown into a confluent monolayer after launch delays.

protocol.sample: Human cancer cell line chosen by the customer (for example FTC-133 follicular thyroid cancer cells, as flown before), about 1e5-5e5 cells per well. Optional fluorescent reporter line for in-flight imaging.
protocol.container: Large bay, 24-well cassette with gas-permeable lids, linked to the bay fluidics (medium, vehicle, drug, fixative and RNA-stabiliser reservoirs, waste bag). Well surface chosen by the customer: standard surfaces if the question is whether microgravity alone drives spheroid formation, or low-attachment surfaces for more even spheroids (these also form spheroids at 1 g).
protocol.launch_state: Cryopreserved at -80 C in the passive cryo cassette; thawed, washed free of cryoprotectant and seeded automatically in orbit
protocol.light_gas: Dark except during imaging. No CO2: HEPES-buffered medium in the sealed bay with gas-permeable lids. No robotic-arm moves during the aggregation days if possible, to keep about 1e-6 g. A lower setpoint (CellBox-2 used 28 C) can be chosen to slow growth.

steps.action: Launch. Cells held at -80 C in the passive cryo cassette. Bay pre-conditioned at 37 C with medium reservoirs filled.
Automatic thaw, dilution and wash to remove cryoprotectant; seed cell suspension into all 24 wells. Baseline brightfield image of every well.
Free aggregation in microgravity. Brightfield imaging of each well every 12 h to count aggregates and measure their size.
Imaging continues. Bay logs temperature, pressure, acceleration and dose so aggregation can be linked to any disturbance.
Automatic partial medium exchange in all wells (Shenzhou-8 and CellBox-2 both exchanged medium 5 days into the flight).
Dosing: 8 wells vehicle only, 8 wells low drug dose, 8 wells high drug dose, pumped from sealed drug reservoirs. Image all wells before and 2 h after dosing.
Daily brightfield and fluorescence imaging (reporter or viability dye) to follow spheroid size and outline under drug. Optional: arm moves the bay to the central 40x microscope for close-up images.

Add a viability dye to a subset of wells and image. Then fix: 12 wells with RNA stabiliser (for RNA and protein), 12 wells with buffered paraformaldehyde (for imaging and histology), 4 of each per dose group.
Replace paraformaldehyde with buffer after about 24 h to avoid over-fixation. Set the bay to 4 C and hold until handover to the courier.

in_flight.name: Spheroid count, size and shape over time
in_flight.method: Brightfield imaging with the bay's LumaScope-class microscope, every 12-24 h, automated image analysis of area and outline

in_flight.name: Drug response trend (growth delay, loss of compact outline)
in_flight.method: Change in spheroid area and outline in drug wells against vehicle wells, from the same daily images

in_flight.name: Viability or reporter signal
in_flight.method: Two-channel fluorescence imaging of a reporter cell line or a dye added through the fluidics before fixation

in_flight.name: Close-up structure of selected spheroids
in_flight.method: Robotic arm carries the bay to the central 40x fluorescence microscope

in_flight.name: Environment record
in_flight.method: Bay temperature, pressure, humidity and acceleration sensors; active silicon dosimeter and passive TLDs

post_flight.name: Spheroid size, number and morphology
post_flight.method: Stereo and light microscopy of fixed wells; comparison with the ground control

post_flight.name: Internal structure and drug effect
post_flight.method: Histology and immunofluorescence of sectioned spheroids (for example proliferation, cell-death and hypoxia markers)

post_flight.name: Gene expression
post_flight.method: qPCR or RNA sequencing from RNA-stabilised wells, including genes reported before (EGF, CTGF, VCL, PXN, ITGB1, RELA, ERK1/2)

post_flight.name: Protein changes
post_flight.method: Western blot or proteomics from RNA-stabilised wells

post_flight.name: Dose received
post_flight.method: Read-out of passive TLDs from the bay

sample_return.note: Samples are fixed in orbit, so no live cells need to come back. On CellBox-2, fixed cells were stored at 4 C. Hold the bay at 4 C through re-entry, recovery and courier transport. Paraformaldehyde is replaced with buffer in orbit to prevent over-fixation. 96 h is our estimate; the customer should confirm it for their assays.

experiments.ground_control: An identical large bay and cassette, with the same cell batch, medium, drug doses and fixatives, runs on the ground at 1 g. It replays the flight timeline and temperature log from telemetry, a few hours behind the flight. This follows CellBox-2, where ground controls used the same temperature and time profiles as the flight. A second ground set on a random positioning machine (simulated microgravity) is optional. Without an in-flight centrifuge, launch, re-entry and radiation effects cannot be fully separated from microgravity.

items.item: 24-well culture cassette with gas-permeable lids, filled
Passive -80 C cryo cassette with cell vials and insulation
Fluidics manifold: micro-pumps, valves, tubing
Reservoirs, filled: HEPES medium, wash buffer, vehicle, two drug doses, paraformaldehyde, RNA stabiliser

module.basis: Our estimate, not a source claim. The 24 wells are needed for three groups (vehicle, low dose, high dose) with two fixation types and four replicates each, which rules out the 12-well medium bay. Peak power of about 28 W happens when the thermoelectric block holds 37 C (up to about 18 W) while the microscope images (about 6 W) and a pump runs (about 3 W). The thaw ramp is scheduled apart from imaging and pumping. Total mass 5.8 kg stays under the 6.0 kg limit.

needs: A low-magnification brightfield objective or a wide-field mode, because spheroids can reach several millimetres (5-10 mm were reported after Shenzhou-8) and outgrow a normal field of view
Image-analysis software on board or on the ground for spheroid area and count

Cytotoxic-drug handling: drug reservoirs and waste kept inside the triple containment, with a materials check that fixatives and drugs do not react with the wetted parts (Shenzhou-8 hardware materials were tested not to inactivate RNAlater)
No robotic-arm moves near the bay during the aggregation days (days 1-5), to keep the quasi-steady level near 1e-6 g
Power after splashdown so the bay can hold 4 C until the courier handover

Optional: an in-flight 1 g centrifuge control for a subset of wells, to separate microgravity from other flight effects (the SIMBOX facility on Shenzhou-8 carried a centrifuge for 1 g reference units)
limitations: Spheroid formation is not guaranteed. The CellBox-2 paper reports that no spheroids formed in the earlier CellBox-1 mission, where cells had become a confluent monolayer after launch delays.

Lab time is 14 days at most. A standard ground spheroid screen (spheroid start, drug treatment, integrity and survival endpoints) takes about 170 h and fits. Measuring growth delay and regrowth after a drug needs 14 days or more of culture, which LELP-1 cannot offer after the thaw and aggregation days.
Spheroids that form freely in microgravity vary in size and number. This makes drug-response data less uniform than plate-based ground screens.
Large spheroids (millimetres across) develop gradients of oxygen and nutrients. This affects drug penetration, and the bay microscope cannot see inside them.
No crew: wells cannot be checked by hand, individual spheroids cannot be picked, and doses cannot be changed except by pre-loaded reservoirs.
Cells launch frozen and are thawed in orbit. Thaw stress and launch loads may affect early behaviour.
No CO2 supply: HEPES-buffered medium only, and pH may drift over 10 days.
Without an in-flight 1 g control, radiation, launch and re-entry effects cannot be fully separated from microgravity.
Cells are fixed in orbit, so live spheroids cannot be brought back for regrowth tests or further drug treatment.
The two heritage flights cited here used one thyroid cancer cell line (FTC-133). Results may not carry over to other tumour types.
Neither heritage flight tested a drug on the spheroids. Drug dosing here is the LELP-1 proposal, not a flown result.

corrections_to_leads: Pietsch et al. 2013 confirmed: Biomaterials 34(31):7694-7705, PMID 23866977. Shenzhou-8 was uncrewed (it carried two dummy astronauts, per Spaceflight Now) and flew for 17 days, landing on the evening of 17 November 2011 (DLR). The cells were cultured for 10 days of that flight: medium exchanged after 5 days, fixed after 10 days.
The Shenzhou-8 spheroids were very large (5-10 mm across, per Warnke 2014), not small aggregates. Warnke compares them with RPM-made spheroids on Earth, not with all ground spheroids.

'CellBox experiments on the ISS' needs care. CellBox-2 (SpaceX CRS-13, launched 15 December 2017, cells returned 12 January 2018) produced spheroids in all six units. The CellBox-2 paper says no spheroids formed in CellBox-1, where cells became confluent after launch delays. We did not verify the CellBox-1 year or launch vehicle, so CellBox-1 is not listed as heritage.

CellBox-2 cultured the cells at 28 C on the ISS, not 37 C. Medium was changed in all six units 5 days after launch, three units were fixed then, and the other three were fixed 5 days later. Fixed cells were stored at 4 C.

Neither heritage flight tested a drug on the spheroids. Drug dosing in this entry is the LELP-1 proposal, not a flown result. NASA's 2017 ADCs in Microgravity investigation was found only as a statement of purpose; we did not confirm published results, so it is not listed as heritage.
